Question No. 47

1.	Was there a radar operator on duty aboard the C.G.S. Baffin when it grounded on Black rock?
2.	If so. did the operator inform the captain that Black rock was ahead?
3.	At what times did he inform the captain about the position of Black rock?
4.	What time was the grounding?
5.	At the time of the grounding, did the captain or the chief hydrographer have supreme control of the ship?
6.	If the chief hydrographer was in control, was he given any message from the radar operator re the position of Black rock?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comfois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
This question is in six parts. The answers are as follows:
1.	No; no one classified as such. Radar watch is maintained by the officer of the watch.
2.	Yes; he informed him the rock was 20 degrees on the port bow.
3.	Exact time not noted; approximately five minutes before grounding.
4.	Exactly 1632 hours; that is 4.32 p.m.
5.	The captain always has supreme control of the ship. The senior assistant hydrographer was directing the course of the ship on a sounding line, from the hydrographers' chart room.

6.	The hydrographer directing the course was informed regarding the position of Black rock when it was estimated to be one and one-half miles, one mile and one-half mile distant.
As a further explanation I may add this. When the captain reached the bridge shortly before the grounding the officer of the watch informed him of the proximity of Black rock. The course the ship was steering at the time would have passed the rock in safety though it would have been dangerously close. The captain went at once to the chart room from which the course was being directed.
In the meantime instructions were given from the chart room to alter the course to 270 in order to proceed to the next line of sounding. This brought the rock directly ahead and the grounding took place before preventive action could have effect. It should be realized that this occurred during dense fog, and the information regarding the proximity of the rock was secured from the radar screen only.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, of which I have given him notice. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON NEW RUSSIAN DISARMAMENT PROPOSAL
speechtext:
I thank the hon.
member for the notice which he gave me a few moments ago. I would first state, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government has not received any communication in this regard. All we know has been gleaned from press reports.
I did say last week that we should not always dismiss out of hand every Soviet proposal, and a communication as important as that which the press report says has been

Inquiries of the Ministry sent to Mr. Nehru, Mr. Eisenhower, and Mr. Macmillan deserves careful study by the recipients and others. I can assure the house that the Canadian government will examine any proposal contained in these letters, if we see the official text. We will examine them with earnest care in the hope that they might provide or offer some prospect of advancement in this difficult and dangerous but essential endeavour to reach an agreement on the measures of disarmament.
We hope, as always we will hope, that the Russians will offer the west something of value. I am bound to say, however, that it will have to be something more solid than a renewal of the demand for simple cessation of nuclear tests. I find nothing, Mr. Speaker, in the press reports which would ensure such observance of such an undertaking, and I would point out to the house, moreover, that the banning of tests is only one part of the disarmament proposals endorsed a few months ago by the United Nations.
These proposals did include the banning of tests which would be effective immediately, but, in addition, that resolution proposed the cessation of the production of nuclear material for weapons purposes and the reduction of conventional armaments and other measures, all under a system of inspection and control which would assure all parties that all other parties were complying with their undertakings.

Article 2 incorporated in the NATO declaration is one that has not received in the past that degree of implementation which many of us would like to see achieved. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subsubtopic: AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY FOR CO-OPERATION IN PEACEFUL USES
speechtext:
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I may make a statement. I desire to inform the house that there was signed earlier this morning an agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany for co-operation in the peaceful uses of atomic energy. The terms provide that the agreement shall come into force upon an exchange of notes to that effect, an exchange which the government intends to carry out later this month. With the leave of the house I shall cause to be deposited with the Clerk copies of the agreement in English and in French.
I do not intend to go into details of this agreement, but I desire to make some comments on it. The agreement was negotiated during September of this year on the basis of a draft prepared by Canada. That draft has been made available to a number of other governments which have expressed an interest in the possibility of concluding an agreement of this nature with Canada. We hope there will be a number of such agreements concluded before long. In this connection I might add that negotiations have been carried on with the government of Switzerland, and we are hopeful that the outcome will be successful and that an agreement with Switzerland will soon be forthcoming and brought into effect.
The agreement with Germany which has now been signed will provide for co-operation between the two countries on a reciprocal basis. That is to say, it does not envisage a
one-way traffic, but rather that each government will assist the other as appropriate and on a basis of equality. The co-operation

involved may take a variety of forms, including the exchange of information, the supply of equipment and materials, and access to and use of facilities. In particular, the agreement will permit arrangements to be made for the supply of uranium from Canada to Germany.
In all cases the activities involved must be directed solely to peaceful ends, and there is provision for adequate safeguards to ensure that materials such as uranium, which are essential to an atomic energy program, shall not be diverted to any military use. I emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker, that adequate safeguards to this end are assured. The safeguards provisions, I may add, are modelled closely upon those of the international atomic energy agency of the United Nations.
I desire at this point to say a few words about the relationship between such bilateral agreements and that agency, of which both Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany are members. Canada wholeheartedly supports the newly established international atomic energy agency, which is designed to encourage, to complement and to assist the efforts of governments, individually or in co-operation on a bilateral or multilateral basis, to develop and apply the peaceful uses of atomic energy. It is quite possible that when the agency is fully operative, as it is not now, the supply of such material as uranium from one country to another will frequently be arranged through it.
As I informed you a moment ago, the statute provides also for bilateral agreements. Provision is made in the statute of the international agency for safeguards in the case of bilateral agreements. The present agreement makes no explicit reference to such an arrangement; neither the international atomic energy agency nor any other suitable international body is yet in a position to apply safeguards, but the possibility of transferring the safeguards functions for which provision is made in the agreement to a mutually acceptable international body is one which could be raised by either party at a later date.
With the leave of the house I am depositing a copy of the agreement with the Clerk of the house.
The terms of the agreement provide that it shall come into force upon an exchange of notes to that effect. As I have already informed the house, it is our intention that this exchange should take place this month. We are confident that this agreement and others like it which may be negotiated with other friendly governments will be supported by all members of the house. I think we can

all agree that agreements of this kind, providing as they do for co-operation on a reciprocal basis, will come to play an important role in the development of the peaceful uses of atomic energy with consequent benefit to our friends and ourselves, and that such agreements will provide an additional market for Canadian uranium.
Finally, these intergovernmental agreements will not in themselves constitute contracts for the export of uranium from Canada. Rather they will establish conditions satisfactory to the two governments concerned under which such contracts may be concluded on a commercial basis between the appropriate governmental agencies in each country. The governmental agencies which will be responsible for the detailed operation of this agreement between West Germany and Canada and the negotiation of any contracts arising under it report to parliament through my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the question addressed to me by the hon. member I am happy to make this statement in relation to the use of nuclear power for peaceful uses.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED PURCHASES BY ROUMANIAN AGRICULTURAL DELEGATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED PURCHASES BY ROUMANIAN AGRICULTURAL DELEGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Medicine Hat directed a question to the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with a Roumanian delegation which was in Canada for several weeks up to about 10 days ago. As reported at page 2127 of Hansard he asked specifically these questions:
What Canadian products were purchased, and has the invitation been accepted?
That is the invitation of the Roumanians to return this visit.
If so, what will the mission attempt to buy or sell?
This agricultural delegation from Roumania was headed by the minister of agriculture for Roumania. In view of the fact that the Department of Agriculture arranged their trip in Canada it is perhaps more appropriate that
[Mr. Johnson (Kindersley).)

I should reply to the question than that the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce should do so.
This delegation was here for the purpose of seeing our methods of farming, and particularly to look into the types of the seeds, livestock and machinery which we have in this country and which might be suitable for use in Roumania. They travelled right across the country and formed a very favourable opinion. They were convinced of the fact that we had here in Canada a good many products which they could buy and make use of.
Whilst they were here they purchased a considerable quantity of hybrid seed corn. They had purchased some hybrid seed corn the year before, and had also purchased some from the United States. They found that our hybrid seed corn turned out better in Roumania than did the purchases they made from the United States. As a result, when they were here this year they purchased something like two and one-half times as much seed corn in Canada as they purchased in the United States on this trip.
They also purchased some hogs; in fact, they purchased a plane load of hogs which were immediately flown to Roumania. It is rather interesting in this connection that the ancestors of those particular hogs were secured from Sir Winston Churchill about four years ago. They also purchased some cattle, Herefords and Black Angus; some chickens and some machinery.
These are all in the nature of what you might call sample purchases. If they turn out to be satisfactory, as I am sure they will, the minister of agriculture for Roumania assured me that they would be back to make considerably larger purchases in future years.
As to the invitation which was issued for a similar delegation to go to Roumania, I assured him that we would consider the matter seriously, and I hope something along that line might be arranged.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED FAILURE OF SUPPLIES TO REACH MISSIONARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet referred on December 3 to a news item in the newspaper he Devoir to the effect that certain missionaries were in distress in the Arctic because their supplies did not reach them this summer. He asked what action the government intended to take.
My answer includes a review of how this operates and then the action we are taking. Supplies for the communities of Igloolik, Repulse Bay and Pelly Bay are norm ally sent by ship from Churchill; supplies for Pelly Bay are taken overland from Repulse Bay to their destination. Unusual ice conditions in Roes Welcome sound this year prevented the Hudson's Bay Company vessel carrying the supplies from reaching either Repulse Bay or Igloolik; the goods, therefore, were left at Coral Harbour on Southampton island.
The failure of ships to arrive is a not uncommon occurrence, particularly at Igloolik,

which in the past has sometimes been isolated tor more than two years. It is, therefore, the custom in such communities to carry reserve stocks to prevent serious distress. There has been no distress either for those living in the community or for the Eskimos trading into them. There are adequate supplies of food and other household requirements.
When the ship failed to arrive, the Hudson's Bay Company arranged for aircraft to fly the supplies from Coral Harbour to Repulse Bay and Igloolik. When they did so they offered to make available space for mission supplies. The material for both the trading store and for the mission at Igloolik has already been delivered. The first load for Repulse Bay will be moved on December 18 and will include 500 pounds of supplies for the mission. The remainder of the store and mission supplies are to go on a second trip in January. subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The resolution before us is one on which a bill will be based that is designed to put into effect our stated program of greater stability of income for agriculture. Its objective is to provide for flexible supports on agricultural products, and to guarantee minimum price levels on key products in relation to prices in a previous base period.
This is a far-reaching and important piece of legislation, perhaps the most important, in its implications, in its expected results for agriculture and its effect on the general economy, that has been considered by the Canadian parliament for many years. I believe this legislation will give to our farmers a much greater degree of security than they have ever enjoyed in our history, but I do not maintain that it is a cure-all


for all the difficulties under which agriculture has laboured for the past several years. No one piece of legislation can be expected, at one stroke, to transform a complex industry, such as agriculture, from a depressed state to one of full and abounding health.
I do maintain that this is a very important step toward that goal. For many years there has been a demand on the part of agricultural organizations and by individual farmers for some form of parity price system in Canada. Exactly what was meant by parity has never been too clear, because its definition varied from organization to organization and from speaker to speaker who dealt with the matter. However, what was generally in mind was some sort of system such as that in effect in the United States, because our farmers were aware that men across the border in the same lines of production as themselves in many cases were receiving higher prices.
At the same time it was common knowledge amongst all who had studied the matter at all that the United States parity price system had led to difficulties of various kinds. It had resulted in the accumulation of vast surpluses of many agricultural products which had proven embarrassing to the United States agricultural economy and government, and the disposal of which has had serious effects on Canada and other nations. The United States system proved unworkable as far as some products were concerned. It produced anomalies and illogical situations in many cases, and it had constituted a heavy drain on the general taxpayer.
In view of all this, as a first step in attempting to devise a practical and workable agricultural prices stabilization bill for Canada I took a fairly close look at the United States system with a view to determining the defects in that system so we might avoid the difficulties which they have run into.
The first and most important defect, I believe, is the lack of flexibility and from this cause most of their troubles have developed. I have endeavoured in this legislation to provide for the greatest possible degree of flexibility so we will not be	saddled with a program which
inevitably acts as an incentive to produce burdensome and unsaleable surpluses. In arriving at the legislation now before you we studied several forms of parity formulae. At this point I should like to pay tribute to the officials of the prices support board, of the marketing service and of the economics division of the Department of Agriculture, all of whom put in a great deal of study and work on this matter. They studied five parity formulae in particular and prepared reports

on them for me, together with supporting documents to show what the effect would have been for each had it been in operation during the past ten years.
From all this mass of material it appeared that the most suitable system for Canada would be one of a three-year moving average as a base period. Among the advantages of the moving average formula is the fact that it deals with the immediate price situation. There is no intermediate step involving the calculation and use of an index. It takes into account technological and other changes, in that the base period advances automatically each year and the base price is adjusted gradually to changing conditions. The base price will be calculated in advance and the prescribed price announced, so that producers will have early notice of the level of support for named commodities and can plan their operations accordingly. Price information is readily available.
The formula is simple and readily understood; and I think this is a matter of great importance, because every farmer in the country can understand the formula, know how it applies and in many cases calculate for himself what the base price is likely to be. Each commodity may be considered entirely independently. The relationship of the base price of one commodity to another is left to the determination of market conditions and is not based on the relationship in some previous period when conditions of supply, demand and methods of production may have been quite different.
The basic reason for recommending a three-year moving average as a base is that the shorter the base and the closer it is to the current market situation, the more accurately it reflects market changes. The three-year average does not perpetuate abnormal conditions for as long as an average calculated for a greater number of years, and affords the farmer more immediate relief.
The purposes of the moving average formula method of determining the base price are to assure stability of income to farmers by protecting them against a drastic decline in prices; to provide for gradual adjustment through prices due to changes in consumption habits, losses of export outlets and radical technological advances, and to provide flexibility so that prompt and desirable adjustments may be made as conditions warrant. This legislation provides that a base price for any agricultural commodity-and I would like to stress the word "any"-will be established by calculating the average price for that commodity at representative markets 96698-139
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization during the three years immediately preceding the year in which the base price is established.
I could perhaps make the matter clearer by citing an example. I would like to emphasize that this example and the figures employed in it bear no direct relationship to actual prices, and this is not to be considered as a prediction or anything of that kind on my part as to what might be done as far as the particular commodity used for the purpose of illustrating the point is concerned; nor is it to be considered as prophesying what might happen in the future with regard to this or any other commodity.
Let us say that the average wholesale price of eggs in 1954 was 45 cents a dozen. In 1955 it was 50 cents a dozen and in 1956 it was 55 cents a dozen. The base price for 1957 then would be the average of these, that is 50 cents a dozen. Then let us say that the average price in 1957 was 60 cents a dozen. The base price for 1958 would be the average of prices for 1955, 1956 and 1957, that is, of 50 cents, 55 cents and 60 cents respectively, which would give a base price for 1958 of 55 cents a dozen. I trust that this brief explanation will have made clear the formula to be employed, the three-year moving average, and will have shown how the base price will be arrived at for any commodity.
However, the formula employed in any system of stabilizing or supporting prices is not what the farmer is primarily interested in; what concerns him, really, are the results, and he wants two of these in particular. First, he wants prices for his products which will cover his cost of production and leave him enough to live on; and second, he desires a sense of security in his price structure, the removal of his long-time fear that prices will fall away to nothing while his crop is growing or his livestock developing to market size.
In this legislation we have attempted to meet these two demands, conditional on not providing a price for any commodity which will serve as a strong incentive to farmers and thus result in large unsaleable surpluses. Guaranteed prices, effective for the next 12 months in most cases, will be set for any agricultural product where the need for such a guaranteed price is shown to exist, except that wheat, oats and barley grown in the wheat board area will not be included.
The reason for this is not to interfere in any way with the operations of the wheat board, which the great majority of farmers in western Canada strongly support. Provision is made that the guaranteed price may be made effective by the board, which the act provides for, through it (a) purchasing the
2188	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization commodity, (b) paying deficiency payments and (c) making such other payments as the governor in council may direct. The legislation provides for the setting up of an advisory committee, representative of farm organizations, which will advise the minister and the board as to what commodities should be placed under price guarantee and what the level of the guarantee should be.
The procedure envisaged is as follows: As soon as possible after January 1 in each year the board will assemble the statistical information necessary and will determine the base price for each commodity under price guarantee, and for others in respect of which it seems likely that price guarantees will be required.
The advisory committee will meet with the board to make its recommendations, and the two will confer together. The board will then make its recommendations to the government as to what commodities should be under guarantee for the next 12 months and the percentage of the base price at which each should be supported. The final responsibility, of course, must rest with the government, which may accept the board's recommendation, alter it or reject it.
In addition to the flexible guaranteed prices which may be applied to any agricultural commodity and which will be the ones in general use, the legislation provides for that sense of security which farmers have asked for and which we believe they are entitled to by providing assured floor prices for certain key commodities. This is done by writing into the legislation a provision that these commodities must be supported under any circumstances at 80 per cent of the base price. It is not expected that these will be the guaranteed prices in effect. The guaranteed prices will be higher in most cases, but this provision is written into the legislation so the farmer will be absolutely assured that no matter how prices may slide he will at the very least receive 80 per cent of the base price.
An example will show how this will operate. Butter has been supported at 58 cents for some years now, and the prices board selling price has been at about that level. Thus the base price will be around that figure. For ease in figuring, let us say it is 60 cents. The guaranteed price for the next year would be 100 per cent of the base price; or if it was desired to raise this a little, which as it happens has been requested during the last month by the dairy producers, the guaranteed price might be 105 per cent of the base price.
At the same time the assured floor price would be 48 cents, so that even if there


should be a catastrophe such as a change of government the farmer would be certain of his minimum of, in this case, 48 cents. So there will be no confusion with regard to the matter I have been talking about I should like to point out that the bill deals with three kinds of prices. There is a base price which is part of a formula arrived at by the use of the three year moving average. There is a guaranteed price which will be in effect for the following 12 months with respect to each of the commodities for which it may be required. Third, there is an assured floor price on certain basic commodities.
To summarize the main features of the legislation, they are: 1. It provides for the stabilization of agricultural prices on a three year moving average formula. 2. Every agricultural commodity, except wheat, oats and barley under the wheat board, is eligible for support. 3. Guaranteed prices will be set as a percentage of the base price in the early months of each year in most cases, and will continue in effect for 12 months after going into effect. The reason I say "in most cases" is that it might happen that in September, August or at some other time a demand would arise for the setting of a guaranteed price for an agricultural commodity which was not under a guaranteed price. In that case the guaranteed price would be set at that time and instead of being for the following 12 months it would be in effect until the next general period for the setting of prices, that is during the first three months of the calendar year. 4. In the case of certain key commodities a price floor of at least 80 per cent of the base price is mandatory under the act. 5. A price stabilization board is provided to carry on the operations of the program. 6. An advisory committee, representative of farm organizations, will be appointed to advise the minister and the board in regard to what commodities require guaranteed prices and the level at which these should be set. 7. A revolving fund of $250 million is available to finance the operations of the scheme.
I have given considerable detail in connection with this legislation, perhaps more than is customary at this stage, but I have done so in order that hon. members may be in no doubt as to what is proposed in the legislation. Further details, I think, should more properly be left for discussion until the bill is in the hands of members and they have had an opportunity to study it. I trust that we may get the resolution through without undue delay and proceed with the further stages of the legislation.

the very large number of parity price formulae which exist, some of them in actual operation in various countries and others which have been proposed, I think they would realize at once that no matter which of these formulae you adopted as a price stabilization basis in Canada there would be all kinds of people, such as those in that group, who would say you should have used another one; you should have used A instead of B or you should have used C instead of X.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a
measure for which the house has been waiting with some degree of eagerness since the opening of the session. I want, in the first place, to say to the Minister of Agriculture that from what he has said I am quite sure he has given a great deal of study to the question. In so doing he has arrived at certain conclusions. I am not going to agree with all the conclusions he has arrived at, but I am going to agree that he has put some time into studying these questions.
This is a question about which we on this side of the house should know something, because we studied it for some considerable time before 1944 when we brought the present act into being. We arrived at the same conclusion at that early time, comparatively speaking, at which the minister has arrived with regard to the United States system. The fact that we did arrive at that conclusion was the foundation for the principle involved in the act which has been on the statute books since 1944.
I am only going to say that after having had a full discussion of the matter, the minister has arrived at the same conclusion as we did at an earlier date. We have only the resolution before us at the moment, apart from the remarks that have been made by the minister, but when I read the resolution I was convinced that there was not very much difference in principle between the

resolution which is on the order paper now and the resolution which was placed on the order paper in 1944, and which is of course available to every member of this house.
The resolution of 1944 went on to state that we were going to set up a board; and it went on beyond that to say that we were providing a system under the act which the board would put into operation. Then we went on to say that there would be $200 million of a revolving fund that the board would have at its disposal from year to year with which to operate.
As I understand it, the present resolution reverses the order a little and that is about all. It says that we are going to set up a system and that system is going to be paid for, as to administration, in the same way it was under the old act. Then it says we are going to set up a board to administer it, and then we are going to have an advisory committee. While I do not think the previous act compelled us to have an advisory committee, we always have had one. That committee has been composed of representatives from farm organizations, with the president of one of them always acting as the chairman. It has included representatives appointed by provincial departments of agriculture across Canada and representatives from the farm organizations themselves.
Those members of that committee were all nominated by either the provincial governments or the farm organizations. None of them were nominees of mine. The only provision in our operation of it was that I had to recommend them to council and council was responsible for their appointment. That procedure was followed in all cases. I did not change any nominee. So we have had an advisory committee running from about 16 I think up to 19 or 20 throughout the period in between, and we have discussed with that advisory committee all matters such as those that are going to be referred to the advisory committee now, and many other matters as well.
That is the situation in so far as the resolution makes it clear to us. In the speech which was made by the minister in introducing the resolution he referred to certain matters. He pointed out clearly the parity price proposals which had been followed in the United States and which were always under discussion in this house when dealing with parity, I think down to last year, both by the official opposition of that time and the other opposition parties of that time as something we should adopt here.
But the present Prime Minister made his position very clear at the time he moved a motion in this house a year ago, a motion
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization which was somewhat different from that which he had moved upon two previous occasions, as to what his position was. On May 16, while he was in the election campaign, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press, speaking at Carman, he referred to the C.C.F. 100 per cent parity policy and after reading it said: "What nonsense; the people of Canada would not stand for it". Then he went on to deal with the ideas he had in mind to bring in. As one of the hon. members suggested in asking questions a few moments ago, he made definite undertakings as to what he was going to bring in. I am not going to try to repeat those at the moment. I have them all here, but I do not think it is necessary to read them all to the house. The house knows fairly well what those undertakings were.
It is true that he has carried out some of them. Only yesterday he announced as the usual means for delay that he was appointing a royal commission to investigate the price spread between farm consumers and farm producers. All I am going to say about that at the moment is that it is just a resurrection of one more of the devices employed by the government of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when he was here years ago. He had the Stevens committee or commission of that time that held meetings all over Canada and then had meetings here in Ottawa at which these very problems were discussed fully.
I am not saying they should not be discussed now. I am only going to point out at this stage that there was a constant review of that situation on the part of the department during all the 22 years I was there as minister; that we had a review every month and every day, from day to day if I undertook to have it reviewed; and I did so whenever questions were raised in the house or otherwise about it. Surveys were made constantly in the different cities and various places across the country, through either the economics branch or the prices branch of the department in order to determine what these positions were.
This government are changing to the extent that they are going to have a commission that is outside the department itself, that has on it representation from certain places, that has on it some persons who can spend their time at that work and arrive at conclusions with regard to the matter. Mr. Chairman, I think on all other occasions when the government introduced a resolution on agriculture, and subsequently a bill, it has always been received throughout the country with a tremendous amount of interest, and certainly this resolution which has been on the order paper since October 25 is no exception. As a matter of fact I doubt whether ever in the history of the industry we have seen such a degree of expectancy on the part of farmers or as much concern with regard to the government's explanation of a resolution.
Certainly that is the only conclusion I can reach based on the large number of letters I have received from my constituents and others, and from conversations I have had with representatives of farm organizations who have been visiting here in Ottawa since the beginning of the session. It is understandable, Mr. Chairman, why there should be this degree of expectancy. It is born of despair and desperation; despair because in the past whenever farm delegations presented petitions to the former government their pleas were always shrugged off, and desperation because the plight of agriculture in this country is such that today there can be no thought of further failure.
Ever since the end of the war, and in particular in the last two or three years, in spite of the fact that when visiting Ottawa farm delegations have used the government's own figures to illustrate the plight in which agriculture now finds itself, the government has turned a deaf ear to their representations and pleas.
The three men most responsible in the past paid little or no attention to those pleas. The former minister of finance merely shrugged his shoulders and said, "The farmers never had it so good". The former minister of trade and commerce was of course always anxious to give us the benefit of his wide business experience. He told the farm delegations that if the farmers could not make a go of it on the farm they had better quit and move to town, but he neglected to say what they should do when they moved to town. The former minister of agriculture merely sat and said nothing.
The latter hon. gentleman, of course, had a plan. He knew there was going to be an election shortly and he realized that something

had to be done. He had been diligently working out a plan that he hoped if carried out properly would re-elect a great many western Liberal members to this house. As the election drew closer he would revise his plan. The plight of the farmer gave him great pangs of remorse. Just before the election, after having jealously guarded this plan and nursed it very carefully, he launched his secret weapon. He put a floor price under old hens over five pounds.
That launching, like another launching of recent date, was also a failure; it fizzled out. I can imagine that the minister must have felt pretty sheepish when he returned to Ottawa following the election, because after all he had hit rock bottom.
Of course this is all past history now, and the agricultural producer is looking forward to this new government doing something for him. Certainly he has every reason to be optimistic that this government is going to do something on his behalf in view of what I propose to read from an official publication of the Conservative party, written over the signature of the Prime Minister, which definitely indicates that he understands the problem.
As a matter of fact western Canadian producers do not expect to receive preferential treatment from this government, but they do realize that the three men now most responsible in this connection come from western Canada, and certainly there can be no excuse for their not knowing the problems which confront western agriculturists. I refer, of course, to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. This is what the Prime Minister said in his booklet with regard to the problem facing the agricultural producer:
The farmer is being squeezed between rising costs of production and falling farm prices. His markets have been lost or diminished because of the ineffective trade policies of the federal government, while, year after year, farm organizations have approached the government with briefs in which the plight of agriculture is set out in detail.
In general, the government has failed to act and has quoted statistics. The farmer's share of the national income has gone down in the last eight years by some 6 per cent and the costs of goods and services that the farmer has to buy have increased by 20 per cent. Furthermore, there has been a continuing reduction in the farmer's share of the consumer dollar, from 59.3 cents of the dollar to approximately 50 cents today.
On the basis of what I have read the farmer realizes that the Prime Minister is well acquainted with current existing conditions in the industry, and he is very optimistic that the government is going to do something in this regard. Further to that I would like to 96698-140
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization read the government's pledge. In this same regard the Prime Minister said to the farmers across the country:
My pledge to farmers in all parts of Canada is:- To assure that the farmer shall receive his fair share of the national income. My objectives will be:-Equality for farmers in Canada's economy. My desire is to correct the social inequity and the inferior economic position into which agriculture has been allowed to fall.
No wonder the farmer has been highly optimistic about the treatment he can expect to receive at the hands of this government; yet after examining this resolution and being both as optimistic and charitable as I can, the very best thing I can say about it is that it falls far short of the producer's expectations in regard to the fair deal he was promised prior to June 10. As far as I can see this resolution represents merely an extension of the present Agricultural Prices Support Act, and I doubt if it is even that good. Even if it were as good, I would point out that that act has been on the statute books since 1944 and has done very little in terms of stabilizing agricultural prices with the possible exception of the price of butter. Furthermore, I would remind hon. members that this act has been roundly condemned on every occasion by those who now form the government.
This morning we listened to the minister make a partial explanation of the resolution. Being as kind as possible to the minister, the best I can say for the explanation he gave is that it is the biggest load of garbage that has ever been dumped on the farmer's doorstep.

Yes. Now, what does the
minister hope this proposed legislation is going to do for the farmer? He hopes for a number of things. First of all he hopes it will give some price stability. His second hope is that it will not be an incentive for the farmer to produce agricultural products. His third hope is that it will protect the farmer against drastic declines in prices. He also indicated that when the need is demonstrated possibly other agricultural products will be taken into account in the legislation. The minister was dead sure of one thing; that under this proposed legislation the farmer will continue to starve, but the minister hopes with a little more dignity than he did under the former administration's legislation.
With all sincerity I say that time is running out on this government. If the bill that follows this resolution does not do more than was mentioned in the explanation given by the minister prior to the luncheon adjournment; if it does not attempt to grapple with the basic problems of Canadian agriculture, then

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the farmer can only conclude that all the promises made by the Conservatives prior to the election were indeed hollow and of little or no value.
What does the resolution propose? We are told it is going to accomplish a number of things but I say it must meet the following four tests. What products are going to be supported? Are these products going to be based on a fair cost-price relationship? Who is going to be supported? Certainly there was nothing in the explanation offered by the minister that would indicate whether the processor or the actual producer is going to be supported. Are these prices forward prices? These prices should be forward prices and certainly the minister gave no explanation as to whether we were going to have a truly forward pricing formula in the proposed legislation. No agricultural legislation can be comprehensive or of value unless it contains satisfactory answers to the four questions I posed.
If we can answer these questions in the affirmative, then surely we are at least halfway to establishing a comprehensive agricultural policy for Canada. Certainly we have to dispose of our wheat surplus and so on, but I maintain that if we have a basic policy such as I have outlined in the four questions I have posed, then we have gone a long way in building an agricultural policy in this country. We have a sort of blind spot with regard to the plight of agriculture relative to the sale of wheat. It is not a question altogether of getting rid of our wheat. If the farmers got rid of all of their wheat at present prices they would still find themselves in a disastrous position. At the wheat pool convention held recently in Regina Mr. J. H. Wesson made this statement:
The farm problem has not arisen primarily from the fact that wheat is not being sold. In the period 1951-56 we sold 168 million bushels more annually than in the previous six year period, but in that period wheat prices dropped 40 cents per bushel or 21 per cent while farm costs rose by 46 per cent.
At the same meeting Mr. George Mclvor had this to say:
Last year alone, because of wider spreads in grade and currency exchange, wheat to the producer dropped 20 cents per bushel.
So it is not just a question of marketing our surplus wheat but a question of price, and that is the important factor. I am not going to attempt to put all the figures on the record, but from 1952 to 1956 farm net income all across Canada fell by 15 per cent. In Alberta it was down 27 per cent and in my own province 31 per cent. Farm prices in Saskatchewan have dropped 28 per cent while farm costs have risen over 49 per cent. 
Last year average farm income in Saskatchewan per individual amounted to around $445. This year it is estimated that it will be almost cut in half and will be somewhere around $225.
That is not brought about by inefficiency but by low prices. We had certainly hoped that in the bill to be based on this resolution that factor would be taken into consideration. The last dominion bureau of statistics figures available show that since 1945 farm machinery has gone up over 94 per cent, other materials over 72 per cent, taxes and interest charges 55 per cent and freight rates 90 per cent. That is why we say we should have a parity price, a price that bears a fair relationship to the costs of production on the one hand and the prices received by agricultural producers on the other.
We also have not been told who is going to be supported under the legislation. Is it going to be the producer or is it going to be the processor? Surely the legislation will provide something better than the present Agricultural Prices Support Act. We know what happened in the case of hogs. When the price of hogs reached the floor the floor was lowered, and so we are looking for something better in this legislation.
I should like to ask the government this question. Has any consideration been given to a two-price system? There again I think many of the farmers' problems could be solved if we were to recognize the importance of introducing a two-price system. I have here a list of products, and out of 14 items there are nine in which we have no surplus whatsoever and two or three others have what is referred to as a manageable surplus. Here is a field in which the government could take action and would have jurisdiction to carry out its program. It would not penalize the consumer.
We should have parity prices for all agricultural products consumed in this country, and it is conceivable that by so doing it would not cost the treasury of the country one nickel. Certainly it would not penalize the consumer, because over the years many farm organizations have produced figures to show that a parity price for wheat, for instance, would simply mean that the increase in the price of a loaf of bread because of the wheat content would only represent 1 cent. I agree that the government would have to take action on the manufacturing level as well as on the producer level under such a program.
We also heard nothing this morning about deficiency payments. I am all in favour of deficiency payments. I realize that in the export field the government has little or no jurisdiction over the prices it receives for

the things that are exported, but I maintain that even in the case of exports the producer should be paid a parity price, and the difference between that price and what the government is able to realize on the export market should be made up to the farmer in the form of a deficiency payment.
When we get the bill we will naturally be able to discuss more fully and intelligently the matters we find in it. With the very brief explanation the minister made this morning and the generalities of the resolution it is rather difficult to deal in detail with the matter. Finally, I simply say that the farmers are going to be keenly disappointed and they are in for a rude awakening if they thought the legislation presented this morning was going to do even a few of the things the government promised it would do prior to June 10.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks I should like to say I was greatly disappointed with the resolution as explained to us by the minister this morning. I look upon the main essential of a support price program as the assuring to farmers of the maintenance of a fair relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices of other commodities. The present proposal appears to ignore that relationship entirely.
What does the legislation actually do? It merely guarantees that the average of the depressed prices of the past three years shall not deteriorate by more than 20 per cent in any one year. That is all it guarantees. It is true the minister stated that the government may decide to set a support price of 105 per cent or 120 per cent of the base price, but there is no guarantee that this will be done. In other words, farmers will have to depend upon the whims of the government in order to get a fair price. Under legislation of that kind you might expect there would be good prices in the year before an election and that the prices would be very poor right after the election. That would be the danger.
What we need is something in the legislation to assure farmers that they will be receiving fair support prices at all times. As to the number of products that will be covered if the legislation remains as it is, I do not think it will make very much difference; but on the other hand I believe the legislation should specify the products that will come under it. I suggest to the minister that the very best thing he could do would be to send a copy of a draft bill to the agriculture committee, call representatives of the farm organizations, let the committee work on a bill, send it back to the house 96698-1401
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization and then introduce it. I do not think he should ask members of the house to give second reading to a bill of this kind merely for the purpose of getting it to the committee. I do not believe he has stated yet that the bill is to be sent to the committee, but I think the government is going to run into very serious criticism from farm organizations if the bill is not submitted to the agriculture committee for their consideration and the calling of witnesses from the various farm organizations.
As I say, all this bill does is guarantee that the average of the prices for the past three years shall not deteriorate by more than 20 per cent in any one year. If the past three years or five years had been good years that might not be too bad a provision; but when you consider that agriculture is a depressed industry-and members on all sides of the house have stressed that fact for a number of years-then to suggest that you are giving farmers adequate protection by assuring them you will not allow this situation to deteriorate by more than another 20 per cent is certainly not even beginning to meet the requirements of the situation.
When you consider that over the past 10 years farmers' costs have risen by 46 per cent while their prices have deteriorated by 7 per cent, it is easy to understand why agriculture today is a depressed industry. You find right across western Canada, and I believe the situation is the same in the east, that the young men are leaving the farms because they are not content to continue to work long hours and take the small remuneration they get as compared with the returns in other industries.
In western Canada you can go into many places and find the farms being operated by old men. The children have left for the city. These farmers find it practically impossible to get labour. This is the situation as we know it in western Canada. I am not saying that some farmers are not prosperous, because some are. There will always be exceptions to the general rule. We believe the immediate need is to introduce legislation that will help stabilize the prices of farm products so they shall bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities.
I know there are many people who oppose the idea of supporting farm prices at a fair level on the ground that it will create surpluses. The minister, in referring to the United States support program, said it had built up surpluses; and that is true. However, this was largely due to the fact they did not have a very efficient marketing system. Let the minister note this fact, that since the United States government adopted

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the surplus disposal program their surpluses are moving out at a taster rate than they are accumulating. The only trouble is they waited too long to adopt a realistic marketing policy. Had this policy been adopted earlier, these surpluses would not have accumulated in the way they have.
I am sure no one would suggest limiting production to the extent that it would merely satisfy our own needs. Any excess of our production should be made available to the nations that need it. Unfortunately that has not been the policy of this government in the past. We have said to other nations, "If you need our products you can have them provided you pay us in dollars. If you cannot, so far as we are concerned you can starve". Our surpluses of wheat are in excess of other nations' ability to buy with dollars, but they are not in excess of the needs of the people of other nations. Even in regard to wheat no one can say that the world surplus is too large. The world surplus of wheat only represents a few months' actual supply, and if the world suffered a series of crop failures we could easily have worldwide famine. Of course the trouble is that Canada holds too large a share of that surplus.
Now, this being the situation we feel that action must be taken to ensure that government agricultural policies encourage and maintain a high level of production of the desired type of products. Provision must be made for storing a reserve of certain farm products to guard against the danger of crop failures, and it is absolutely essential that steps be taken to see that that reserve of food be not allowed to force the prices of farm products below economic levels. Trade policies must be instituted to make it possible for Canada to make these surplus farm products available to nations that are not able to obtain them through the normal channels of trade.
Whenever the question of support prices is raised you will always find some people who criticize the proposal. You invariably find editorials in eastern newspapers, and unfortunately in some of the western newspapers, criticizing a policy of what they call giving the farmer a hand-out. We in this group have always maintained that the farmers have a right to demand support prices for their farm products. It will be recalled that in the latter years of the war the prime minister of that day, the late Mackenzie King, pointed out that at that time farmers were being compelled to accept less than the world price as a result of government policy. He said this was part of a stabilization program and they would guarantee, as part of
[Mr. Quelch.l
the post-war policy, to stabilize the prices of farm products so they maintained a fair relationship with the prices of other commodities.
As a sign of good faith the Agricultural Prices Support Act was introduced. There is one serious deficiency in that act. The Prime Minister had promised to maintain the prices of the main farm products, yet for some reason or other wheat was not covered by the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Wheat is unquestionably one of the main farm products in Canada today. Had wheat been placed under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and had the formula that has been used under that act been applied to wheat to the full extent, then the price of wheat would have been $2.37 a bushel. That is a figure given by the bureau of statistics.
Let me say a few words about the Agricultural Prices Support Act as we have it at the present time. I have always supported the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I think it is a good act if it is used to the fullest extent possible. I recall that in January, 1951, I think it was, the former minister of agriculture spoke to a convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He was asked to define the formula for setting prices. I am not using his exact words, but I believe he said it was the intention to maintain the prices of farm products so they would bear the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as existed in the base period 1943 to 1945. Personally I think that was a good formula. My main quarrel with the government is that they have not lived up to that intention to the full extent. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture advocated the base period of 1925 to 1929, but actually the period 1943 to 1945 gives a 1 per cent advantage over 1925 to 1929.
Unfortunately the government have not maintained the prices of farm products today at 100 per cent of parity for the base period 1943-1945. As of January this year the support price on butter was 81 per cent of parity for that period; the support price on hogs was 80 per cent of parity for that period, and the support price on eggs was 54 per cent of parity. What will the new proposal given to us this morning mean? Well, these parity prices I have given are approximately the same for the past three years, so those would be the average prices for the past three years. Instead of the farmers getting 81 per cent of parity on butter they would only get 80 per cent of 81 per cent or only 64 per cent. Instead of getting 80 per cent of parity on hogs they would only get 80 per cent of 80 per cent or only 64 per cent. Instead of getting 54 per cent of parity on

eggs they would get only approximately 43 per cent. So under the new formula the farmers will not be anything like as well off as they are under the present formula.
It is true that the present formula is not written into the act and the formula proposed by the minister is to be written in. But I would prefer to operate under an unwritten formula that is fairly satisfactory than to operate under a formula that is written into the act but that is far from being satisfactory. I suggest to the minister that this act should be sent to the agriculture committee before the house is asked to give it second reading, because when second reading is given members must endorse the principle of the act.
I do not like the principle of the act, because it does not guarantee to the farmers a fair relationship; and unless a support act can guarantee that fair relationship it is practically worthless. It raises the amount of the revolving fund from $200 million to $250 million. That does not appear to be very important, because although we have had a revolving fund of $200 million in the past the total costs up to date amount to $99 million, and $70 million of that amount was in connection with foot-and-mouth disease, so that in the period from 1944 to 1957 only $29 million has been used in so far as support prices are concerned. There is therefore no reason to assume that just because the revolving fund is raised from $200 million to $250 million it will mean that larger amounts will be paid out.
In western Canada many farmers felt that the government had committed a breach of faith on the question of support prices. They had been assured by the former prime minister that if they did not object too strongly to having to have a ceiling on their farm products during the war, they would be assured stabilized prices in the future. They assert, and I think rightly so, that that promise was not lived up to. As a consequence, the last election fairly well liquidated the Liberals in western Canada.
The Conservative party was very critical of the Liberals for failing to enable the farmers to obtain their fair share of the national income. That was one of their main election promises. The Prime Minister has stressed the urgency of raising the farm standard of Living by a program of support prices, expansion of markets and the increasing of terminal storage. I would agree with the Minister of Agriculture that support prices alone cannot rectify the situation. All these three things are necessary. But I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the attitude of
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the Prime Minister on the question of support prices at the last session of parliament, when he moved a resolution as follows:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given to introducing during the present session of parliament legislation which will assure farmers support prices for agricultural products based on a fair price-cost relationship.-
And that amendment was then amended by adding the words:
-thereby resulting in agriculture receiving its reasonable share of the national income based on parity.
The Prime Minister supported that resolution and the Conservative party voted in favour of it. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would not suggest that the present legislation can in any way guarantee what the resolution of the Prime Minister was aimed at achieving.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the individual farm unions recently presented quite valuable briefs, in my opinion, to members of parliament, and in those briefs they have advocated support prices and deficiency payments to agriculture. I believe both these things have their part to play in any agricultural program.
First of all, support prices should be set early in advance of the year in which they are to become effective. This support price should be on the basis of parity so far as the domestic market is concerned. We believe that exports should be sold at the best prices obtainable on the world market, preferably under international agreement. Then to the extent that the aggregate of sales in domestic and export markets fails to provide to farmers their fair share of the national income, deficiency payments should be made.
That, of course, is a two-price system. Whilst it might take a little time to put a two-price system into operation so far as all agricultural products are concerned, it would be a comparatively easy or simple thing to apply the two-price system in so far as wheat is concerned, because all wheat is sold through the wheat board. The wheat sold through the wheat board in the domestic market would be sold at parity, and the rest would be sold at the world market price and the farmers would receive an average of the two in the final payment.
I know some people are critical of the idea of a two-price system, but after all if they are critical of agriculture for asking for the adoption of a two-price system, they should be critical of all the secondary industries which have operated under that system for as long back as I can remember. Secondary industries set their prices internally at a price that will give them the cost of production and a fair return on their investment.
2200	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization Then to the extent that they have surplus products, they are exported abroad at the best price that can be obtained; and very often the prices obtained for the products exported abroad are considerably lower than the prices charged in the domestic market.
Agriculture unfortunately or, I might say, primary industry on the other hand has not been able to carry that policy into effect. As a matter of fact we have found that whilst about 94 per cent of all farm products apart from wheat are consumed in the domestic market, the small percentage of 6 per cent that is exported abroad has set the price for the 94 per cent that is consumed in Canada. In other words we allow the tail to wag the dog.
We believe that the most efficient way in which to operate that two-price system would be through marketing boards; and as I have already pointed out, it would be quite a simple operation in so far as the wheat board is concerned. In so far as marketing boards have been established on a provincial basis, it might be possible to apply the two-price system through those marketing boards, but it may be quite a while before the farmers throughout Canada are prepared to sell all their produce through marketing boards on the same basis as the wheat board. We therefore feel that in the meantime ways and means should be found of applying the two-price system without the operation of marketing boards. There are many ways in which the two-price system can be applied without waiting for marketing boards to be established.
To those people who have the idea that it would not be fair to charge the people in Canada a higher price than is charged externally, may I say this. Let them remember that when the farm organizations advocate a two-price system, and advocate that the price on the domestic market should be at parity, by parity they merely mean a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities.
Is any member of this house going to say that the farmers in Canada are not entitled to receive for their products sold in Canada a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities? That is all they are asking. Certainly they would like to have a parity price for all their farm products, but we have no control over the export market. We cannot control the prices in the export market, but we can control the price internally.
We are therefore urging upon the government the desirability of establishing a two-price system so that in the domestic market the prices on the different markets


shall be such that it bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities, no higher and no less, and then get the best price we can in the world market. Then if at the end of operations for the year we found there was a serious disparity between the national income and the farmers' share of it, deficiency payments could be put into effect in order to remove that disparity.
I am not going to say any more at this time, Mr. Chairman. I think my time is fairly well up. I appreciate that this is not an easy problem to solve. I would therefore urge upon the minister the desirability of sending the bill to the agriculture committee in the form of a draft bill.
There are plenty of precedents for that. Back in 1945, when we drafted the veterans' charter the government sent those bills, before second reading, to the veterans committee and told it to work on those bills and redraft them in whatever shape the committee thought necessary. The committee did that; they made many changes in the bills and then the minister, meeting us in camera, told us to what extent he was prepared to meet the changes we had advocated. He went quite a long way in that regard.
Now that was a new procedure, I believe, at the time but every veteran member who has spoken in this house since then has praised that procedure because, as a result of it, we got a veterans' charter which is probably as good as any to be found in the world. I believe if the Minister of Agriculture would adopt that policy in regard to this bill we might have a bill which would meet and would earn the approval of all the farm organizations in this country.
