speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about the resolution under discussion at this time which provides for a considerable increase in the amounts appropriated for the administration of the agricultural prices support act.
This morning I followed rather attentively the remarks made by the Minister for Agriculture (Mr. Harkness). I must say that I was a little disappointed at the way in which the government plans to go about solving the problem of price support. That is why I hasten to submit a proposal which I believe constructive and which I commend to the minister's earnest attention. Here is what I have in mind. With certain products, it just will not do to announce only twelve months in advance at what level the price will be fixed. On several previous occasions I have pointed out that in so far as butter is concerned, more particularly, the producer should

be able to rely on a fixed price for a long period ahead of time, so as to plan his production and determine how much he should spend on improving his stock, for example, without risking a dead loss.
To my mind that is a basic principle of sound farm management, one which indeed has been recognized in the past, for it was in 1953, I believe,-I did not have time to check-that the government fixed for three years in advance the support price for butter.
There is no doubt that, particularly since the end of 1955, it has been hard going for the farmers of this country. Recently the report of the Department of Agriculture mentioned that their gross income would be greater in 1957 than in 1956. However, their net income will be lower because of higher costs of production. The farmer's immediate prospects are therefore not very rosy.
Then, too, it is now recognized that the welfare of people generally, throughout Canada, is intimately bound up with the welfare of the farmer. In the constituency of Beauce more particularly I think it may safely be said that there is a very close relationship between the position of the farmer and that of the other groups, workers, employees, storekeepers and manufacturers, and that the prosperity of these people is largely dependent upon the revenue of the farmer.
Now, among the sources of revenue of farmers in the constituency of Beauce, the maple sugar industry stands out both in respect of the number of people who are engaged in it-42 per cent approximately-and of the revenue it provides, which equals that secured from all other forest products combined. It must be noted here that for the last two years this industry has been in a very depressed state. May I just say at this point that because this product is marketed largely outside the province that produces it, and especially outside Canada, I believe it is the federal government's duty to help solve the problem of marketing this product.
According to reliable surveys, it costs about 25 or 26 cents to produce a pound of maple syrup. Well, this year, the sale price has ranged between 15 and 22 cents a pound. Last year it was a little higher, but far from satisfactory. The situation is therefore intolerable and it is hardly surprising that, for two years now, many maple sugar producers did not even bother tapping their trees, and some producers even decided to chop them
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization down. In my opinion, it is most undesirable to let an industry die out whose raw material, labour and equipment are distinctly Canadian. I do not believe I am overstating the case when I say that if the maple sugar industry ever disappears from the county of Beauce, nearly half our farmers will quit the farm.
I am glad to be able to say that maple syrup producers have tried and are still trying very hard to put up a solid front to the buyers. Some of them are members of the Societe cooperative des producteurs de sucre (sugar producers' co-operative), an excellent organization. The Catholic Farmers' Union, for its part, has taken on a huge job, for which it deserves congratulations, in developing a joint marketing plan with the cooperation of the provincial marketing board. A new group, still not fully organized, the Syndicat des producteurs de sucre (sugar producers' union), has only recently entered the field but has already achieved creditable results which, though not spectacular, are undeniable.
Last summer, when the Societe cooperative was able to pay 18 to 21 cents a pound, because of a guarantee provided by the federal government with the help of public funds, independent producers had to sell to dealers at 15 cents a pound, or risk having to keep their product indefinitely. I repeat here what I stated during the last electoral campaign: "This procedure constitutes, on the part of the government, serious discrimination against a considerable number of producers". And that is where the support price, to which I will come in a moment, would have provided equal opportunities to all. In the light of these facts, I felt it my duty to do all I could to help those unjustly treated producers by supporting the activity of the new union. They held out so firmly that dealers thought it wise to raise their prices gradually and I can say that, for two or three months, they are paying almost as much as does the Societe cooperative itself. There is no doubt in my mind that this is largely the result of the unremitting efforts of the sugar producers' union.
However, in spite of the work and good will of all concerned, the problem is far from being solved and I urge the government to give us their co-operation.
On March 28 last, as well as before and after that date, through representations to ministers of agriculture, I asked here for the establishment of a support price, just as the

2202	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Landry) did himself in this house on October 18 last. After having his departmental experts study my suggestion, the then minister of agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) advised me that it was not accepted. To be factual, I must say that, at the time, the parties concerned were by no means in perfect agreement.
I may add that for the past few months opinions have changed and that the great majority of producers I have met, and with whom I have discussed the problem, now think that the government should establish price support. The Catholic Farmers' Union itself, at its 33rd annual convention, recommended to the federal government the establishment of a support price of 25 cents a pound for maple syrup. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am on very good ground for renewing my request for a price support which, in my estimation, should be at least 25 cents.
Now then, if I come back now to what the Minister of Agriculture explained to the committee this morning, and if I take the average of prices paid in the last three years, namely 1955, 1956 and 1957, I get an average price of 26J cents. On the other hand, if I take 80 per cent of that 26J cents, the result is 21 cents a pound. And if I should be as optimistic as the minister was this morning, and take 105 per cent of this base price, I obtain a guaranteed price of 27.1 cents a pound. I would hesitate to believe that the minister will always be so enthusiastic and that he will set the base price at 105 per cent which, as I said, would represent, in the case of maple sugar, 26 cents for the three years. I doubt very much that this percentage would be granted the producer. It would set a guaranteed price of 27 cents a pound, which is just about what the producer of maple sugar and the Catholic Farmers' Union have been asking for. Some of those who are against this price support measure have argued that, to all intents and purposes, this support price would become a ceiling price. The answer to this objection is to be found in what has happened with the sale of pork. While the support price of this commodity was set at 23 cents, as hon. members know, its selling price this fall went up to 35 cents and, if I am not mistaken, even to 37 cents a pound.
A few words now on the problem of the price of butcher cattle and calves. In this field, unstable prices are very harmful to producers, and not only to those who specialize in raising this type of cattle, but also to

owners of dairy cattle. Indeed with the increasingly careful selection practised nowadays, every dairy herd includes a large number of heads which are classified as substandard and must be slaughtered. And when you think of how much it costs today for feed -and the same could be said of fertilizers- you will easily understand that the raising of beef cattle is hardly a paying proposition for the dairy owner. It will often eat up any profit he might have made out of his dairy herd. The same is true of the production of butcher calves.
For those reasons, I strongly suggest to the hon. minister that he very carefully consider this problem, and that the experts who will make up the advisory committee, as provided in the resolution also give their most careful and early attention to my proposal of a support price in the case of butcher cattle and calves, as well as maple syrup.
And now I want to say a few words about other products already under a price support which, I feel, should be brought to a higher level. First, as far as butter is concerned, a support price of 58 cents might have been adequate around 1952 and the following years, but is obviously no longer so today, considering the increased costs of production. This problem, however, presents a new aspect which we cannot afford to overlook if not only the producer but the consumer as well are to be protected. Indeed, I believe that, as I have said many times in the past, if the price of butter to the consumer was held for several years at a reasonable level, it is because the government, through price support, has piled up huge stocks. This, I might say, is a constant threat to the speculators who might have been tempted to create an artificial shortage with consequent unjustified and unfair prices to the buyer, and, of course, without any profit to the producer either. Just remember what happened during the winter 1951-52. After just such a scandalous manoeuvre by speculators, the retail price soared to 85 and even 90 cents a pound, while the producer of course got nothing whatever out of this exorbitant increase.
Now, according to the figures given to the house by the hon. Minister of Agriculture on the 5th of this month, butter stocks have been dwindling steadily for the past three years. From 92 million pounds in 1955, they fell to 81 million pounds in 1956 and to 34 million pounds at the end of last November. Without being much of an econbmist, I think we just reached a danger

point and that we are on the threshold of an early and serious shortage, which is bound to touch off an unfair rise of prices at the consumer level. To protect the buyer, butter stocks, in my opinion, should be built up, and I think that the only practical way to make this possible would be to raise tne price support to 63 cents and even to 65 cents a pound.
And there again, if I refer to the hon. minister's report, and take as a basic rate the average price paid to farmers in the last three years, I find that this is not very hard to figure out. We have now 58 cents; if we take 80 per cent of 58 cents, we get a price of 46.4 cents a pound, which, as the hon. member who preceded me just read, is the only real guarantee now given by the hon. gentleman in the introductory resolution. If, on the other hand, you get all excited about the way the Department of Agriculture is going to establish this price, and if the basic rate is raised to 100 or 105 per cent, you get a ceiling price of 60.9 cents a pound. This is indeed far from the floor price requested by the Catholic Farmers' Union at their 33rd annual convention.
Knowing the minister's almost anxious hope that his bill will go through with the shortest possible delay, hon. members will understand that I am summarizing as much as possible a discussion that would call for far more explanations.
And finally, one last word to suggest that the support price for pork be raised at least to the level it had reached over the last few years, that is 26 cents for grade A.
I know that this year the prevailing price has been far above the support price. However, there are signs now of a declining trend and there is a possibility that sooner or later that trend will gain momentum and reach the floor price which, at the present time, is unquestionably inadequate. In the last few weeks, I have talked over this matter with several Beauce farmers, and all of them agree that, considering the cost of labour, of building piggeries, and especially the cost of feed, 23 cents is altogether inadequate.
Against a raise in support prices, it was claimed that too high a price would induce a lot of people to go into hog breeding, who have now no interest whatever in doing it.
As a matter of fact, experience has shown that industrialists, business men, merchants, and even lawyers and doctors have gone into hog raising and, incidentally helped prices to come down by causing a surplus on the market.

I would have a suggestion to offer to do away with this difficulty, and that would be to limit the number of heads which each breeder would be allowed to deliver to the board in a given period. The limit would be set by experts and could vary from year to year and even from district to district. Hon. members will please note that there would be no question of limiting production, but only the number of heads delivered to the board. This would certainly eliminate breeders who are not bona fide farmers, who do not need to raise hogs to earn a living and who are interested in this type of production only so long as they can organize it on a large scale, to reap considerable profits. This would hardly be possible with the system I am suggesting.
I will close on that remark while at the same time expressing the sincere wish that the measure under discussion may really prove helpful to the Canadian farmer and, at the same time protect the Canadian consumer.

Then, paragraph (c) of that subsection is in these words:
(c) to pay to the producers of an agricultural product directly or through such agent as the board may determine the difference between a price prescribed by the board with the approval of the governor in council for such product and the average price, as determined by the board, at which such product is sold in the market during a specified period if such average price is below such prescribed price.

I am not surprised at all at this. With all the talk that has been put out in the country, on the basis of which the hon. members were elected, and all the hopes held out, and then the introduction of this measure which does not carry the legislation any farther forward than it was before, I am not surprised that they attempt to do everything to prevent these facts being brought out.
Somebody may say, well, you people had this legislation and why did you not raise the income of the farmer so it bore a fair relationship to the income received in other occupations as is provided for in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. One of the difficulties about raising the prices of agricultural products much higher than world prices was that if you did that you had then to impose strict import controls and practically bar the importation of agricultural products into Canada. It was realized, as the Prime Minister stated when he was leader of the opposition, that if you started doing that you were, in spirit in any event, going against the general agreement on tariffs and trade. If you start doing that, you can expect reprisals from other, countries. The farmers themselves have always taken the attitude that we wanted to expand our trade; we did not want to get into a trade war. All our policies in trying to get the farmers' prices up as high as possible were instituted with the fact in mind that we could not start a tariff war.
I have here a copy of a statement of policy issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, adopted on January 26, 1956. This

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization statement of policy frankly faces that situation. I am reading from page 7 of this statement of policy:
A country like Canada also has this special problem-that in the case of some commodities it attempts, for sound reasons of national policy, to maintain a domestic level of prices that is above the world level. At the same time it desires to look to the world market to dispose of limited quantities of those commodities that will not be absorbed at home at those higher-than-world levels. The United States also is in this position, with a scale of production and surpluses far in excess of Canada's.
It should be possible for Canada to export these commodities, in fairly limited quantities, in regular world markets and at world prices. But it must be recognized that this type of operation must be carried on with discretion, and with consideration for regular exporters of these products, and for our obligation under GATT.
The situation must also be looked at from the point of view of Canada's position as an actual and potential importer of farm products.
Where it is necessary to support the price of a product, it may sometimes be necessary at the same time to take steps to control imports.
Then, they go on to make recommendations, and two of their recommendations are:
1.	Canada should continue to pursue a national policy aimed at achieving the freest possible flow of trade between nations.
4. The multilateral negotiation of agreements on tariffs and trade practices, as achieved under GATT is in principle sound and should be continued. Some formal organization for the administration of GATT and for facilitating international co-operation on trade problems is also desirable.
This was the attitude of this organized farm organization as they approached this great problem, so I presume it was the attitude of the advisory committee headed by Mr. Hannam. It did tend to keep prices from being raised higher than might otherwise have been the case under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a submission to the members of the government on July 31 of this year. This problem has come to be realized more and more by everyone including the farm organizations. If you want to expand trade, if you at the same time want to raise prices on farm products high enough to give the farmers a fair share of the national income, you will have to raise them a good deal higher than they actually are in international trade and that would mean that you would have to impose import controls. If you begin to bar out imports, then other countries will begin to bar out our exports. This was finally realized by many people who were thinking about this problem. This is something I wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. I presume that he has studied this submission of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture very carefully. It was as I have said made to the government of which

he is a member on July 31 of this year. I read from this brief because it indicates a realization that something more had to be done than had been done before and it asks for something more to be done. It seems to me that the government which promised to do more than had been done previously, should have paid some attention to this submission which I consider most reasonable. At page 3 of this submission to the government the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said this:
In January of 1955 a statement of policy was adopted by the federation of which the major features were:
1.	That price supports should not create incentives to production which perpetuate surplus production problems and prevent necessary and desirable production adjustments being made. This is the most fundamental principle involved, next to that of providing for the producer due and reasonable safeguards against excessive loss of income.
2.	That price supports should be calculated according to a known formula, embodied in legislation, which could be used as a guide, accepted by all concerned, for negotiating price supports.
3.	That as a general rule between 70 and 85 per cent of a fair relationship or parity level, as calculated by the formula, would provide for a reasonable range of supports, with due regard for flexibility. With supports established at such moderate levels, it is recognized that market prices will usually prevail above support levels and sometimes substantially above them.
4.	That deficiency payments as a method of price supports were not to be recommended in preference to market price supports-except with rapidly perishable products.
That was the position of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture up until practically this year, namely that deficiency payments should not be used and were not desirable except for rapidly perishable products. Then this brief of July 31 last goes on to say this:
The above remain the basic principles of C.F.A. price support policy except with respect to deficiency payments. The arguments against the use of deficiency payments unquestionably have a considerable degree of validity, and in a general way the federation prefers the market support technique where it is practicable. At the same time the advantages of supporting producer returns by means which do not involve maintaining market prices at the full support level are very real and since the beginning of this year a special national committee has been reviewing this particular aspect of price support policy.
Last week the board of directors of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture received the report of that committee-
They say "last week". That would be the last week of July of this year.
-and revised its statement of price support policy. After a thorough review of the question, it was decided that adjustment or deficiency payments as a method of supporting incomes of producers should be applied on individual products to correct income deficiencies under the following circumstances:
Here the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said that they have changed their

attitude towards deficiency payments and have submitted this new and most reasonable recommendation to the government. I expected that the government meant business when it said it was going to do something about this great problem. Here is what they said: that they should be used
(a)	Where perishable products require this type of support in order to move the product and avoid waste.
(b)	Where market price supports, though put at the best level feasible for this type of support, must be supplemented from the point of view of providing adequate producer returns.

speechtext:
Before I proceed with my remarks, Mr. Chairman, please permit me to congratulate Mr. Speaker and you as Deputy Speaker on your election to the important offices you hold. I also wish to commend you both for the kind, courteous and impartial manner in which you have steered the deliberations of this house. I wish to express the same sentiments towards the clerks and those that assist us in the house.
There is one misgiving which I feel I should share with you Mr. Chairman, and hon. members of this house and that is the difficult role I have to fill in representing the constituency of Marquette in Manitoba for the following reasons. My immediate predecessor representing this finest of Manitoba constituencies was Hon. Stuart S. Garson who, for nine years, distinguished himself as minister of justice in the late Liberal government. His predecessor was the late Senator James Allison Glen who for a number of years occupied the chair which you, sir, are now occupying. His predecessor was the late Senator Harry Mullins whom many of the oldtimers must remember. You will now believe me, Mr. Chairman, when I say that the mantle of these outstanding Canadians weighs heavily on my shoulders and I pray to the Almighty for ability, strength and vision to serve Marquette and Canada as ably as did my predecessors.
I want to make the definite statement that we are proud of the proposed legislation, as proud as we are of the legislation we have put on the books to date. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on his manner of presenting the principles of the bill to be introduced after the resolution passes, if it does so. He was concise, brief and to the point. He expressed the hope that this legislation would not be unduly delayed, and I share his hope. Consequently I am not going to take up too much time of this house as lengthy speeches will only result in delay. I hope that the bill which will soon be in our hands will contain, if not all at least most of that for which the farmers have been waiting for so many years.
I cannot resist expressing certain opinions and views on the resolution which introduces the price support legislation, which legislation is of such vital importance, not only to
2210	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the primary producers of my own constituency but those of all other constituencies. Indeed, all the primary producers of Canada have desired price support legislation; the economy of the country requires it and I am sure all groups in this house agree with the principle behind it.
The farmers comprise one-sixth of our population, this one-sixth providing one-quarter of our exports. These are the farmers of Canada, whether they grow grain, raise hogs, poultry or cattle.
Labour, being well organized into unions, has been clamouring for and receiving increases in wages and other benefits while this one-sixth of our population, the men and women on the farms, were until this government came into power the all but forgotten group of this country. When they asked in years past for just such legislation as this they were told it was impossible; it could not be provided; that nature would take care of their surpluses by several years of crop failures and then eventually Canadians would eat up these surpluses.
If this has a familiar ring in the ears of some hon. members 1 hope they will not be too disturbed. The farmer never knows whether or not he will harvest a crop. If he does not harvest a crop he has nothing to sell and therefore has no income in the fall. If he has too big a crop the prices fall and so does his income, a surplus then being created. This situation applies to whatever type of farmer one might consider but even if he can sell his produce prices fluctuate and he can never budget for his needs in advance. For example, there was a fluctuation in hog prices last summer, with a difference of 10 to 12 cents in a period of a few short weeks. These are the reasons why farmers in the whole of Canada have been so anxious for so many years to see this legislation introduced.
Referring again to this one-sixth of our population, taking for the moment the farmer and his wife and leaving aside the children, these people work from dawn to dusk, at times during all hours of the night. Both husband and wife work seven days a week for 365 days a year, with a day extra in leap years. They have no holidays with or without pay. They never know in advance what they will receive for the fruits of their labour and this is why farmers sell out and our farm population is dwindling. The farmer goes into the industrial centre, increasing the labour force, and soon swells the ranks of the unemployed. Therefore, this one-sixth of our population must read with envy our debates in this house on the matter of the minimum wage of one dollar per hour. I submit that if the farmer, anywhere in Canada, billed his farm at the rate of one
[Mr. Mandziuk.l

dollar per hour, at the end of the year he would have a bill to the tune of over $5,000. That is for both himself and his wife and I daresay there is not a farmer in my constituency or, for that matter, in any other constituency who clears that much money for his labour on 365 days a year. I say this because of the unstable prices and the surpluses which exist.
The farmer's wife cannot enjoy the finer things of life; she cannot have clothes as good as those of her sister in the city; she cannot have household appliances such as those owned by her sister in the city and she cannot enjoy all the conveniences enjoyed by her sister in the city, even though that sister may be the wife of a labourer. The farmer himself cannot afford to dress as well as his brother who is a labourer in the city. He wears the same suit for years- probably the suit in which he was married- and he may even be buried in the same suit. His products are priced at a certain figure; his surpluses cannot be sold and he has no ready cash. I therefore believe that the farmer certainly appreciates the cash advance legislation which we have already passed and will likewise appreciate the price support legislation we are about to pass.
The farmer cannot buy as good a car as his labourer brother who lives in the city. Who but the farmer still drives the old flivver of the 1940 or 1945 model? All this, in spite of the fact that they have lived through that great prosperity under the Liberal government. I could point out tens of hundreds of such old model cars in my own constituency. Do you know why we cannot afford to get new ones? Because there is not the money available and these old models are not valuable enough to be used as a trade-in. Now these are efficient farmers and a car in these days is a necessity and not a luxury.
I am just trying to give a picture of the farm situation today and I think all hon. members will understand why this legislation will be appreciated. This uncertainty as to prices is bad for the Canadian worker, although he may not realize it. It is bad for the manufacturer if one-sixth of our population has no buying power. A prosperous agricultural community would provide a substantial market. The implement industry for example has remained in a depressed state since 1949; that started in the good old days of the grand Liberal administration. The crisis in agriculture is also bad for the small town businessman in every constituency in Canada. It is bad for the grocer, the general merchant, the implement agent and the automobile dealer all of whom depend upon local patronage and the buying power

of their customer-the farmer. It is bad for the wholesaler. If the retailer sells less, the wholesaler sells less then the manufacturer must reduce production in his factory and his workers are laid off. Then the hue and cry is raised: "What is the government going to do about it?" The legislation of this government is an important answer to this question.

speechtext: And how!

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have heard that before- it is doing that which should have been done years ago. The primary producers have cried for such legislation; they have asked for it again and again over the years but their cry was a voice in the wilderness. I feel that the people whom I have the honour to represent will be pleased-no, much more than pleased,-they will be happy at the courage of this government in going ahead with the legislation, going ahead with what others said could not be done. My constituents consist of small farmers, small town businessmen and they will be looking forward to the benefits which are expected from this legislation. They will get those benefits in 1958.
I was glad to note that the government is acting like a servant of the people rather than like a master. I was very pleased with the support which hon. members representing constituencies in the east gave to legislation beneficial to the west alone, that is, to the measure providing for cash advances on farm-stored grain. We who come from the west did not have to convince the eastern representatives that this legislation was worth while; they felt that what was good for any one section of Canada should be supported by the whole of Canada. This government realizes the interdependence of every section of the country and this realization will, I am sure, result in a united and more prosperous Canada.
I promised to make my remarks brief, and I will keep my promise. In closing, I feel sure, sir, that this government will go down in history-

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must admit I am on the spot today perhaps more than I have ever been before. I had prepared a speech for this heavy occasion, this great occasion to which I have been looking forward for years, and now I cannot even use it because it would not fit. I expressed the hope that this would be the day which would save agriculture. And now, after listening to the Minister of Agriculture speak about this incredible and shocking proposal which has been revealed here, this speech of mine would look silly, coming after his.

speechtext:
Just think if I had used my first sentence:
I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this resolution which is the forerunner of legislation to bring greater stability to farm prices.
That is what I thought this was going to be. Now what is it? It is nothing. According to the minister's statement, the prices for the year will be based on the prices prevailing during the last three years, which were about-estimated conservatively-80 per cent of parity. Thus, he will base the new prices on 80 per cent of the 80 per cent. A joke. Just think if I were to read another sentence of my proposed speech:
For a long time I have been waiting for this day when a government would recognize the problem of low farm prices and do something to stop this process which is crippling a basic Canadian industry.
Just think how silly that would sound. I do not even know with what to compare, or how to describe this thing which was revealed this morning because my vocabulary is too restricted. Perhaps the only thing I can do is to compare it with the United States sputnik which they tried to launch into the air a few days ago; the size of a cantaloupe, six point four inches in diameter, weighing three point four pounds. Never got off the ground. Exploded in their faces. It fizzled out, but it produced a shock wave right across this country unprecedented in history and this proposal, similarly, will create a feeling in the hearts of farmers of despair and chagrin. And this is what follows all the beautiful promises.
To think I have been one of those who advised my friends to vote for the Conservatives to get rid of the Liberals. Just think what they will do with me when I get home. What a spot a man can get into in life. I do not even know where I go from here. I cannot go on speaking freely; I must use a script, but the script I have prepared does not fit the occasion. If I do not use a script, what will happen to me? What,

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization for example, will the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources do with me?
I never used a script in my life until I came to this house, but I use one now because I know that someone will be out to catch me. But I never thought the minister of northern affairs would do it. But that minister went out and distorted the truth and said I was the man who said that legislation for advance payments was useless. Why did he not read my speech before he made such a statement? Of course he said yesterday that I said it was stupid, and that that was just the same. Yes, it was "stupid" that appeared in Hansard, but I went up the next day and corrected it. When I said I had corrected the proof and did not use that word, what right had he to go out and say I had used it?
I have heard a lot in my time about the present minister of northern affairs. I have heard a lot of his statements, and most of them were so confused that I could make neither head nor tail of them. I have read a lot about him, too, I read an article the other day which, perhaps, fits the occasion, and I should like to quote it. It is taken from the Toronto Star of November 15 and, describing the minister of northern affairs, it says this:
Among the minuses goes Alvin Hamilton from Saskatchewan, minister of northern affairs. This is a pity, since there were high hopes of promise in this freshman minister (who incidentally was just nosed out for a Rhodes scholarship by his own deputy minister, Gordon Robertson). But at question time Alvin Hamilton adopts the manner of a youthful prig-
That is spelled p-r-i-g.
-rebuking his elders. But he is so new to the commons club that he may yet revise his manner and bring forward substantial material. Better hurry, though.
Yes, he had better hurry because if he does not history will count him with the group of people who leave as their footprints in the sands of time only the mark of a heel.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to protect myself against further distortions of the truth by making use of my script. I do it for another purpose as well. It was my main purpose today to describe the present condition of agriculture and perhaps there is still some hope that the Minister of Agriculture will listen to my remarks and go back and think them over. If he does, we will even forgive him his sins. However, I will not leave out, of course, all those hopeful expressions I have used.
During the years farmers have been faced with many problems and even crises which they have managed to overcome but low and unsuitable prices for farm products represent


a problem they have been unable to solve. As a matter of fact, this problem has increased in proportion year after year and has now reached the point where farmers are helplessly caught in the iron jaws of the present rise in costs. It is a problem of such magnitude that it has brought the Canadian agricultural industry to the brink of collapse, something this country can ill afford.
Agriculture not only served this country well but it played an important role in its development. The dynamic expansion of agriculture provided investment opportunities and became a major drawing card of immigration and colonization. With the opening of the western farm region agriculture became the foundation of the Canadian nation. Today this foundation is threatened by falling farm prices and rising production costs which have reduced many farmers to bankruptcy in the midst of prosperity. Consequently Canada's basic industry has become the weak spot in our economy. The reason for this is that the Canadian farmer was not only ignored by those who planned the distribution of this country's wealth but became an object of abuse. While industry was protected by tariff walls and finance was supplied with cheap money the farmer was left as booty for the speculators and manipulators of trade and commerce. While other groups were protected, he was forced to sell his products on the open and unprotected market where he was taken advantage of in the most unscrupulous manner. Looted for years, this builder of yesterday was slowly reduced to the point where today he is becoming the most puzzling and pathetic contemporary figure. The man who had been the backbone of our country, the very prototype of Canada, finds himself at present on the social and economic fringe. While many Canadians prosper, he can scarcely make a living.
Since 1949 the farm price index-basis 1935-1939 equals 100-declined from a high of 255.4 to a low of 224.0 in April 1957, a drop of 31.4 points; but in the same time the composite index of prices of commodities and services used by farmers went up from 204.1 to 258.6, a rise of 54.5 points. Both rise and fall combined represent a total loss to the farmer of 85.9 points in a little more than six years. This is the day when our new Minister of Agriculture has announced that the government will offer price supports. The condition I have described is the product of social chaos and economic lawlessness which produced the imbalance in our economy, prosperity on one side and bankruptcy on the other. This is the way in which the farmers were cheated out of their livelihood. This is the manner in

which this great prosperity of ours was built on the ruins of our basic industry. It is an unprecedented piece of economic chicanery.
If this kind of discrimination had occurred only in the last few years farmers would not be in their present bankrupt position; it takes much more time to bring them to their knees but this is a sort of nightmare the farmers have been living with for years. It would be interesting to know how many years but apparently there are figures available only since 1914. I paid a visit to the parliamentary library and there I found the Searle index of the cost of things prairie farmers have to buy for a living and production, together with some other indices and prices of interest. The index goes back to 1914 and provides a startling comparison for the next 25 years. The period 1913-14 equalling 100 was used as a basis for calculation.
It shows that in the first ten-year period the cost index of things farmers buy increased from 100 in 1914 to 163 in 1924, but in the same ten years the price index of wheat went up to only 124-a difference of 39 points. The index for hogs went down to 94; this is 69 points behind the cost index. The price index for cattle fell from 100 in 1914 to 78 in 1924, which is 85 points below the cost of production index.
Ten years later in 1934, at the time of the depression, the farmer's cost index had fallen to 124, but the price index for wheat went down to 72, close to half of the cost index. The hog index fell to 94, 30 points below the cost, and that of cattle dropped to 47, or 87 points behind the cost of production.
In 1939, the last year shown in the index, the farmer's cost was up to 132, but the price of wheat went down to 64 points, less than half of the farmer's cost. The price index of hogs stood at 105 and that of cattle at 91. That means that in 1935 the combined average price of the three main products which provide approximately 65 per cent of the prairie farmer's income was 45 points below his cost and 13 points lower than in 1914.
The full significance of these figures and the amount the farmers actually lost in those 25 years can only be seen in its full dimension when you compare it with what other groups have gained in the same time. According to the index, the hourly wage rate of industrial workers increased from 100 in 1914 to 188 points in 1935. This means that while farmers' prices went down 13 points in 25 years, industrial wages went up 88 points. It produces an imbalance between the two groups of 101 points. This figure represents
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the difference in living standards between industrial workers and farmers brought about in 25 years, and the industrial workers as a group by no means have the highest standard of living in this country.
Will the public in general ever recognize the tragedy embodied in these figures? This is an incredible testimony of discrimination and injustice. It should penetrate like a depth bomb into the hearts and souls of those who hear and read this manifestation of fraud. I hope it penetrates into the heart of the Minister of Agriculture. It is a gigantic social upheaval in its own right, covered up by beautiful phrases describing our unprecedented prosperity in the most glowing terms. But when this idol of prosperity is stripped to public gaze and its grisly secrets revealed it becomes a farce of the greatest magnitude.
Under a chaotic economic system, with no resemblance of order or balance, the tiller of the soil has been ravished and deprived of his labour for decades. There is something sinister about this age-old piracy which has left farmers helpless and hopeless. It degrades human dignity and what we have heard today degrades morality.
To stop-perhaps I should leave out this paragraph-this repellent suppression and correct the existing discrepancy, the government is now forced to introduce legislation to guarantee farmers prices by the law of the land. What a law!
Will hon. gentlemen support this new measure? I hope they will not. I have been one of those who tried very hard to give the government a chance. As a matter of fact, sometimes I have even disagreed with my own good friends here because I felt the people of the country expected us to give the government a chance. They have had their chance. I do not feel sorry for those on the treasury benches but I certainly feel sorry for those who sit behind them.

Farmers in general are rugged men and know how to stand on their own roughshod feet. Their successful struggle with nature and the task of transforming a wilderness into a productive industry stands out in Canadian history as an epic of determination. They do not expect either a hand-out or something for nothing. All they want is a square deal, and I doubt whether they can ever expect to get it from this government unless the government has a change of heart.
I hope the figures I have produced so far will have some effect but if they do not and there are still some doubting Thomases who

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization are still not quite sure as to the conditions that exist in agriculture today, I have here some more definite figures. A survey conducted by the economics division of the Department of Agriculture in west central Manitoba last year and published in the Economic Annalist of June, 1957, shows that farmers must receive assistance or they will all go bankrupt in the near future. The report states that the area in which the test was conducted reached from Neepawa west and north of Russell. That is the constituency of Marquette represented by the hon. member who spoke just before me. What did he say? He said that he was proud of this legislation.

speechtext: He will eat those words.

The area surveyed included 82 farms of 2, 3 or 4 quarter sections. The report states further that the area is generally considered as a mixed farming area and is well suited climatically for common cereals. The average annual yield of wheat is about 25 bushels per acre. The net result of this investigation is contained in the last paragraph which reads as follows:
The returns on two-thirds of these farms fell in the range from about $1,290 to $3,210. The average investment on the two quarter-section grain farms was $18,848 per farm, which at 5 per cent would earn, or cost, $942. This leaves a return of $1,117 for the operator for wages and management, family living expenditures and savings. Farm family living expenses were not enumerated in this survey, but data collected in earlier studies suggest that cash farm family living expenses for families on this size of farm would amount to about $1,550 per farm. On the average, these farm families, on this size of farm, would have to use some of their depreciation allowances, savings, or income from non-farm sources, such as family allowances to meet all costs of farming, including their living costs.
This is the measure of the farmer's plight, a net loss of $433 in one year. It really proves the falsehood of our prosperity, of which some people are so proud, especially when one considers that according to the report livestock products and meat consumed in the home were included as receipts and that the expense figures include cash expenses and depreciation but do not include cash expenses for machinery and equipment.
Furthermore, we must remember that this applies to the year 1955 and that according to a report recently published by the Manitoba department of agriculture the average net income of Manitoba farms in 1956 fell about $1,000 below that of 1955. This brings the total loss per farm to $1,433. Is there anyone anywhere who can tell me how these people can go on without going bankrupt? Can anybody figure out how they live when their expenses are greater than their income? I cannot do it and neither can anyone else.
Will the hon. member for Fort William- I should have said the Minister of Agriculture


this time-be able to understand from now on what we mean when we talk about thousands of bankrupt farmers and ask for assistance? It is not only the farmers but whole communities that have been impoverished by the cost-price squeeze. Toiling under the most impossible conditions farmers and businessmen alike are struggling desperately to keep their heads above water.
Unfortunately, Canadians in general, and I think that applies to this house in general too, as well as some farmers and farm organizations, have so far failed to comprehend the extent of the depression existing in agriculture and the threatening danger it presents to our entire economic structure. While the nation's foundation is crumbling they build their castles in the clouds of prosperity. They have been brainwashed to the point where they really believe in this myth.
The only group really concerned about this problem and which has repeatedly stated so publicly is the Canadian Labour Congress. In the last brief this organization presented to the government it was made quite clear that the congress was alarmed by the drastic fall in farm income as that was bad for the economy in general. They assured the government of their full support for anything the government could do to restore the purchasing power of Canadian farmers.
This is not the first time organized labour has asked the government to recognize the farmers' difficulty and do something about it. Last year they combined their efforts with those of the interprovincial farm union council in a joint representation to the government asking for parity prices. However, there was no response from the former government. They acted like a group of people made of clay and tied in a bag that no one could undo.
But how much will this government do now to correct this situation? This is the $64 question to which farmers want an answer. I hope this government realizes that it was a Conservative government that laid the groundwork for the farmers' present dilemma. Back in 1879, a Conservative government designed the national policy of tariff protection which spelled doom for agriculture from the first day of its existence. The unprotected farmers have been forced for 78 years to compete with a protected home industry. Farmers realize today that they cannot expect any reduction in tariffs from a Conservative government, and therefore they are asking for protection too. Since coming into office this government has demonstrated that it is more interested in raising tariffs than in lowering them. Farmers know that the idea of free trade, promoted

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
by them from the very beginning, is not acceptable to this government. This was proven conclusively when the offer of a free trade area made by Britain was greeted with silence and has been ignored ever since.
The organized farmers of today, therefore, have made up their minds to get equality with others, either by free trade for all or protection for all. They want protection of prices to the point where they have a fair relationship with other prices. They know that this is the only way in which they can get a fair share of the national income as promised in the speech from the throne. They are asking for the establishment of a price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers as laid down in the government's national election policy. Farmers want parity prices as promised by the Prime Minister during the election campaign. They are asking for implementation of what they have been promised-no more or no less.
Farmers and farm organizations are looking forward with great expectation to this legislation. As far as they are concerned the government will stand or fall on its context. They want a degree of price protection equal to other prices. This means parity prices. Anything less will be rejected, not only by farmers but by labour and many others who know the difference between right and wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was with a certain amount of anxiety and with a great deal of expectation that I, too, have been waiting for the time when we would be able to have a thorough discussion of this farm problem. I, however, was not in the same position as the hon. member who preceded me because I, perhaps, remember too much of the thirties so I only had to throw out about half of my speech when the announcement was made.
The resolution introduced by the Minister of Agriculture today provides an opportunity for the agriculture industry to state its grievances, so far as farm prices are concerned, and to express views upon what they expect to see in the bill when it is introduced. As I mentioned during the throne speech debate, about 90 per cent of the people in my constituency are dependent, either directly or indirectly, on the agricultural industry. It is, therefore, of prime importance to them. The farm holdings are not large ones. The problems that face agriculture are not prevalent only in my constituency, these problems face the entire agricultural industry
throughout this country to a greater or lesser degree. Perhaps at the outset I should state that I do not believe legislation, even though it might be a lot better than the measure proposed this morning, would cure all the ills of the agricultural industry.
I would say that the first thing we need is trade, and we need it badly. However, under the conditions in which farmers are now placed, and until such time as the government sees fit to inaugurate different trade policies, legislation to give support to agricultural prices should be introduced in order that the farmers may survive. I was very much interested when, just before six o'clock last Saturday, December 6, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that the acceptance of local currencies for wheat may be adopted if it were a solution to getting our surplus to the hungry people of the world who need it.
I was very much interested in that because on October 23 I asked the Minister of Finance whether the government had given consideration to the acceptance of sterling in an effort to increase trade with Britain and other commonwealth countries. The minister answered that no such proposals were made to the Canadian government. There was a significant statement made by him when he was further questioned by other members of this group and by some members of the C.C.F. group. He said then he did not see any reason why we should go out proposing to take sterling; we were interested in a two-way flow of trade and payment by commodities that are being purchased from noncommonwealth sources. In other words, the Minister of Finance is prepared, I believe, to do a bit of bartering.
The sad part of the whole affair is that these statements come from the wrong minister. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is prepared to do business with soft currency countries, and that is the department of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance is prepared to do a little bartering, and that is within the Department of Trade and Commerce, but he will not have anything to do with sterling. If ever I or anyone else has seen a mixed up government I believe this is it.
I shall not go into this subject any further now because I intend to go into it more fully when the trade and commerce estimates are before the committee. I would suggest, however, to the Minister of Agriculture that he should get the two gentlemen together and get the whole matter straightened out. If that fails, perhaps he could convince the Prime Minister to have these gentlemen exchange

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization portfolios. I believe both these ministers have expressed sound ideas, based on good common sense. I believe some of the old Social Credit members must derive some satisfaction from these statements because they have been hammering away at these ideas ever since the Bretton Woods agreement. If the Minister of Agriculture were to recommend that we accept foreign currencies, barter deals, extend credit to foreign countries, that would do more than any one single item of legislation we could possibly pass in this house to aid this farm industry.
Before I go too far with that, I shall come back to the resolution and deal directly with it. The problem that the farm people have of balancing their diminishing returns of income against their ever-increasing expenses is not only causing an endless amount of anxiety to the Canadian farmer but is becoming a subject of study to other groups and occupations.
The Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944-45 was supposed to have remedied the situation and it is very clearly stated in one of its clauses that the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
This is only fair and just. It is no more than any farm group or any farmer has ever asked for. Farm people do not want handouts but they do want and are entitled to their fair and just share of the national income. Whether it is the fault of the agricultural prices support board or whether it is the fault of the governor in council, I am not prepared to say. However, the blame must lay with those who were given the responsibility of seeing that the act was enforced.
The resolution introduced today calls for guaranteed prices on certain agricultural commodities, and others can be added as named from time to time by the governor in council. The wording may differ slightly. However, the ideas are identical with those we have had in the past. The amount of authorized expenditure from the consolidated revenue fund will be increased to $250 million, an increase of $50 million. We trust that the $50 million increase is not just so much eye-wash or that the government is not merely trying to pull the wool over the farmers' eyes but rather that the government really and sincerely is trying to aid the agricultural industry. I say that with justification.
The following question was placed on the order paper on November 19, 1957 by my colleague, the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose:

1.	How much was paid out of the Agricultural Prices Support Act revolving fund for each of the years from 1946 to 1956 inclusive?
2.	How much was paid out of the Agricultural Prices Support Act revolving fund from January 1, 1957 to October 31, 1957?
3.	What products were supported in each of the years mentioned in 1 and 2, and what was the loss incurred for each of these products for each of these years?
I will not read the detailed reply. You will be able to find that in the December 2 issue of Hansard at page 1756. However, the total in round figures for the ten-year period or the better than ten-year period I believe will be of interest. The total cost up to October 31 since 1946 was $94 million. Of this amount the biggest loss occurred in 1952 when we had the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, slashing returns to the producers. These figures do not take into consideration the value of goods still in storage such as eggs, butter and so on so that the total amount for the ten-year period is much below the $90 million, and much below what some of the former government members try to convince the farm people the aid actually was to the farmers. When we subtract that amount that we paid out in 1952 for the foot-and-mouth disease, it leaves about roughly $24 million for actual farm aid.
I have here the report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act as put out by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The amount of assistance given to that industry is found at page 10 of that booklet:
The amount of money paid to gold mines in respect of the years 1948 to 1956, inclusive, under the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is $99,934,837.10 on a production during these years of 28,603,429.035 ounces.
When we consider what we are doing we find that we are digging the gold out of a hole in one place and placing it in a hole in another place, something which is of absolutely no value to the people of this country and for that we paid out $99 million. Yet when we take our farm commodities, what do we find? I am not going to argue the point as to how this was brought about because I was not here when this act was passed. I do not know very much about the gold mining industry and I am not going to say it should not be paid out. But I am just comparing the situations. In the one case we have this gold being taken out of one hole and put in another hole, and we have this amount of money being paid for something that benefits nobody.
Yet when it comes down to the agricultural industry, there is little or practically nothing done. The actual amount spent under the prices support act is about $24 million. The $200 million voted by the previous

administration was nothing more than just a frill to the actual amount needed to carry out the obligations of the board or the actual amount spent. As to adding $50 million to the fund as proposed by this present administration, unless the guaranteed prices shall be such as will use up the money in this fund, and unless the board shall see that the . prices are of benefit to the industry, it shall become nothing more than adding embroidery to the frills.
The previous administration did not carry out its duty in seeing that the prices support act was adhered to. As I mentioned previously, I will not lay blame on any particular body, but I do know that the farm people have the right to expect certain justice. When an act is passed, they expect it to be adhered to. I am not a lawyer so I shall not attempt to argue as to whose fault it was that it was not adhered to. I have no argument with any of the members of the board. I do not know them. I also believe

as the Minister of Agriculture said this morning, or something to this effect-that the men holding positions on this board are qualified and responsible men. However, if it was the fault of the board in not carrying out their responsibility, they should have been asked to apply for unemployment insurance.
I am not saying that is where the fault is. If it was the fault of the governor in council in not issuing a directive to the board members, I believe they should resign because they have not only failed the agricultural industry in that department that they should represent, they have also failed parliament. If the administration itself is at fault it can and will be dealt with as the former administration was dealt with last June. The only drawback is that the people of this country can deal with such injustices far too seldom to prevent a number of their group losing out entirely. I trust that the present administration will bring in this resolution with amendments as suggested by the hon. member for Acadia, and that it will not be just so much eyewash or just so much wool being pulled over the farmers' eyes but that it will contain real meat and be of benefit to the farm people and consequently eventually to the benefit of our entire economy.
It has been known for a long time by our economists that whenever a basic industry in any country becomes depressed it affects every other industry. It is also known that unless the basic industries are in a sound financial position, regardless of what is done to bolster subsidiary industries those measures eventually become futile in trying to stabilize the economy of the country. It is most unfortunate for the farmers of this
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization country that agriculture, being a basic industry, is one of the first to be affected by adverse conditions. Agriculture is in the unfortunate position of most basic industries in a country in that when conditions become adverse it is not only the first to be crippled but is usually the one that bears the brunt of the blow. It is also unfortunate that when conditions improve the agricultural industry is usually the last to receive any benefits of any of these improvements. It therefore should be the aim of any government to see that the basic industries, the very foundation of the economy, should be in a sound financial position.
This however, has not been the position in the agricultural industry of this country. It has not been the position, furthermore, for the past several years. The decline in farm incomes during the period of rising costs has at the present time forced the agricultural industry into an extremely depressed condition. I have at hand letters from different farm people and farm organizations. I do not wish to take up the time of the house by reading them all but it is a similar story everywhere. Now I have letters from farm union locals in the Smoky Lake area, that is to say Barich, Smoky Lake, Victoria north bank, Pakan, Edward, North Kotzman, Wild Deer, South Kotzman and the Ruthenia, locals which resolved as follows:
Resolved that we bring this matter before the House of Commons and bring prices up to a fair value.
The farm union local at Innisfree has this to say:
Whereas the majority of farmers at the present time are operating at a loss and cannot continue to do so much longer, we resolve that some steps be taken to better the financial conditions of the western farmer.
Now I am afraid that the bill, as proposed in this resolution, will not do that. I can only hope that the bill will be amended and will be different from what is contained in this resolution.

Now this is not peculiar to my own constituency. Nor does it only apply to a particular section of Canada; it applies generally to the industry of the nation as a whole. It is not a situation which has developed overnight, but it has been one of progressive deterioration until, today, we have a primary industry, the resources of which have come to a point which is causing our farm people a great deal of anxiety. It should be given a great deal of consideration by this government.
Perhaps we should have a look at some of the figures. The net farm income for 1951 was $2,155 million. This is a decline to where, in 1954, we see a drop of 48 per cent to $1,125 million.
Now then, according to the brief presented to the former minister of agriculture by the interprovincial farm union council, the picture in western Canada was even worse. In 1951 the net income was $1,227 million; by 1954 it had declined to $376 million, or a drop in the net farm income of 66.6 per cent. The situation has since improved only slightly. Whereas in 1951 the farm people obtained 13.6 per cent of the national income, by 1954 this percentage had dropped to 6.8 per cent and by 1956 had only increased to 6.9 per cent.
Against this farm income there has been an ever-increasing rise in the farm family living costs. Whereas in 1946 the price index was 100, it has since then been rising almost constantly to a point where in 1956 it was 162.2, and it is still rising. The real income in terms of 1946 constant dollars has risen from $1674 in 1955 to $1686 in 1956-a rise of $12 for the average farm family. All the indications are that when the figures are available for 1957 there will be no appreciable change.
Now this resolution which was brought in this morning by the Minister of Agriculture is going to be based on a three year moving average and there is absolutely no hope that I can see where these people can get out of the situation which faces them today. If we take the three previous years, the net farm income, measured in constant dollars, was $1,674, $1,686 and $1,300 in 1954. So we can expect the average is going to be $1,600. Well it will not even be $1,600 for the farm family in agriculture. Now that is what is being proposed as a basis for prices for farm people in Canada today.


With the ever increasing prices and everything else which must be considered, what chance have the farm people? That is why I believe the Minister of Agriculture should give thought to the suggestions of the hon. member for Acadia in bringing this matter before the agricultural committee in order to consider some of these things thoroughly before the second reading of the bill, where . it must be passed in principle.
Farm prices are now and have been over the last several years completely out of balance and unless that balance is restored as between farm prices and farm costs the diminishing buying power of the farmer will be reflected in the entire business life of the country and will contribute to the increasing labour problem to an even far greater degree than is evident today.
We recommended that grain be included among the products covered by the Agricultural Prices Support Act but the minister this morning mentioned that no such thing would be done. We further recommend the full application of section 9 of the present act so as to ensure that the support act will maintain the price of the farm product at a level which bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities.
I say this because the farmer today is not competing with the farmers of other lands; the Canadian farmer must compete with the treasuries of practically every other wheat producing country. The Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned in the house a couple of weeks ago that Canadian wheat was selling for 11 cents a bushel more than was the wheat of any other country. It is interesting to note what our Canadian farmer receives for his superior quality wheat and what the farmers of other countries receive for their wheat. The following figures are extracted from the brief presented to the cabinet on March 9, 1957 by the Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta wheat pools:
Ireland, $2.06: United Kingdom, $2.31; Belgium, $2.56; Japan, $2.59; Austria, $2.63; United States of America approximately $2.08 (it was $2.24); Brazil, $2.85; Germany, $2.73; Italy, $3.05; Norway, $3.43; Switzerland, $4.03.
Those are the prices per bushel. Now with respect to Canada, the price is $1.40 and that is after the farmer has delivered it to Fort William.
Mr. Graham Spry, Saskatchewan's agent general to the United Kingdom, told the delegates of the Saskatchewan farmers union last Wednesday that the subsidy received by the farmers of France was greater than our Canadian sales price. How then can the Canadian farmer compete against such prices in the open market? How can the Canadian

farmer compete against the treasuries of these different countries and against the treasury of the United States, without government support? I hope the minister will see fit to place grains under this act.
We recommend a two-price system; we advocate that support prices be maintained at 100 per cent of parity for farm products sold on the domestic market and that the surplus products be sold abroad for the best price available, preferably under some form of international agreement but covered, in any event, by a price support sufficient to meet the average costs of production.
I believe this has been partially covered by other members of our group but, in view of the fact that 94 per cent of all farm products, excluding wheat, are sold in Canada, it would mean that farmers would receive 100 per cent of parity for 94 per cent of their products, again of course excluding wheat.
In regard to wheat, approximately 80 per cent is sold abroad and 20 per cent in the domestic market. Therefore, 20 per cent at parity of $2.37 per bushel, which I believe was the figure mentioned, and 80 per cent at the ceiling of $1.95 per bushel-under the international wheat agreement-would give the farmer a support price of $2.01.
Those who believe such prices would create surpluses to an even greater degree than we have today-I believe something along this line was mentioned by the minister this morning-entirely miss the problems of agriculture.
The Food and Agricultural Organization, whose meetings the minister himself attended in Rome not too long ago, is on record as holding the opinion-though this statement has been made earlier-that surpluses exist only in relation to purchasing power and not in relation to the actual needs of human beings. The problem was in the distribution of these surpluses. Numerous people have expressed this idea, and if I have read the record correctly, hon. members in this group have done so in the house ever since 1935.
The latest person to express such a view was none other than the Prime Minister himself, as reported in the Wheat Pool Budget of August 16, 1957, when he said:
To those who think that in agriculture we have arrived at a point where we need no longer expand I say to you this:	I learned one lesson at the
commonwealth conference in London. We must expand our agricultural development. With one quarter of the world's population going to bed hungry at night, methods must be found to enable the distribution of our surpluses to the end that happiness will come to the peoples of the world.
These are not the comments of a wheat pool delegate or an Alberta farm union official, they are the words of the present 96698-141
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization Prime Minister spoken to 11,000 people at the opening of the Saskatoon exhibition on July 22.
I should like to turn briefly, now, to a problem in relation to cattle about which I cannot agree with the Minister of Agriculture. On November 14, I addressed the following question to the minister, as recorded in Hansard at page 1106:
In view of the drastic drop in livestock prices, has the government been in consultation with representative farm organizations to arrive at a definite formula for adequate price supports? If so, will such a formula be proposed for enactment this session? Is the minister aware of the urgency of such legislation, and does he intend to introduce such legislation without delay? And being aware that the small producers are planning their next year's production now, is the minister prepared to issue any directive to the farmers of Canada today?
When the minister gave me his answer that day I thought for a while that he was deliberately evading the issue, or maybe he was trying to make me sound a little silly, but after hearing today's resolution I realize that that was not the case.

Mr. Chairman, the last speaker said he thought this resolution should go through quickly and there should be no debate on it. I feel that is not the case. I think this problem needs a lot more discussion so that the go\ernment will know exactly what the farmers' situation is. The Prime Minister comes from an agricultural province and he promised, during the election campaign and for years before

that, that if he ever got an opportunity the farmers would receive their fair share of the national income. I have carefully read the resolution which is before us, and I could read it again but I do not think that is necessary. It is quite lengthy but I might point out there is not a single word in it which indicates the farmer will get his fair share of the national income under this measure.
The resolution says, in part:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a system of guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities-
What does that mean? These guaranteed prices could be away below parity. There is nothing that says they shall be up to the point where they will give the farmer his share of the national prosperity. I, for one, am greatly disappointed. When 1 left home in October to come down here a lot of people in my constituency said to me, "Give the government a chance; give John Diefenbaker a chance". On many occasions I have remained in my seat when I would have liked to take part in the discussion. I have been waiting and hoping that when this legislation, which was mentioned in the speech from the throne, was brought down we would have something that would give to our farmers what they have been looking for for many years. I have been fighting for a square deal for the farmers for 40 years. I fought the Liberals for a good many years. When we got them out of the way I thought we would have some hope with this new government because they would want to make themselves popular out in the country amongst the farming people. We hoped this government would bring forward legislation which would give to the farmers their share of the national income.
I feel very strongly about this. I feel so strongly, in fact, that if the Minister of Agriculture cannot persuade me, between now and the time we have to vote on this resolution, that the measure will be effective I feel inclined to vote against it right now. I cannot see a great deal of improvement in this measure over the old Agricultural Prices Support Act. As I said before, I am disappointed that the government has not seen fit to take steps which would give to our farmers a square deal. The hon. member who preceded me said there was no need for discussion. I might point out that I have lots of figures on my desk, but I am not going to go over them. Surely there have been enough figures put on the record today, during this session and last session and for the past five years, so that every member who has been here for any length of time knows what the problem is.
From 1951 to 1955 there were some 47,000 farmers who were forced to leave their farm
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization homes. Since then there have been probably another 3,000 or 4,000. This means there have been over 50,000 farmers who have had to leave their farms during the last six years. What does that mean to our economy and to our farming districts?
I am more familiar with the situation in Saskatchewan than in the other parts of Canada. I have a very good friend who sits on the government benches, who is a farmer coming from Ontario. I have discussed the farm situation with him a good many times, and he has told me that there is hardly a young man left on the farms in Ontario. I have seen many vacant farms when I have been driving through this province.
There were two reasons why the farmers left the farms during the last six years, and one of them has been the cost-price squeeze. The other reason has been mechanization. The smaller farmers and even the middlesized farmers have been forced out of business. If they had been getting fair prices they would have been in business now. What is the result of all this? Our country schools are closing down. In our own province some thousands of schools have been closed in the rural areas. This situation is spreading into the villages and towns today. There are many villages in my province in which the schools have had to be closed because there have not been enough children to support the schools. The children now are taken by bus 15 or 20 miles to a point where there is a school.
It is not only the farmers who are affected but the businessmen. What is happening to the small businessmen? I wish the Minister of Agriculture would take a little time off and drive through some of the little towns to see what is happening to the small businessmen. They are closing their doors, and there is hardly a village in western Canada today that has not some empty stores in which businesses had operated profitably for years. All at once the population disappears, and they have to go out of business. This is a serious problem. As I said before, I am disappointed that the government has not seen fit to introduce the legislation which they promised would give the farmer his share of the national income. Until the government does this, the government is not going to be supported by the farmers of this country.
