They were looking forward with a great deal of hope, and with considerable optimism, feeling secure in the knowledge that some of these promises would be kept. I think, too, the members of this house looked forward with a degree of optimism when we saw this resolution on the order paper and when we had been told continuously by leaders of the government that we should proceed with all haste and not waste the time of the house so that this great piece of legislation, this cure-all for the ailments of the farmer, could be presented. It was presented this morning. I am satisfied that every member of this house, except the most partisan, was keenly disappointed.
We listened to the words of the minister in explaining that resolution. I am going to say that this resolution looked quite good but the more he explained what actually was intended to follow, the worse it seemed to get. He used a couple of phrases that stuck in my mind. One of them was that this is most important in its implications. As far as implications are concerned, I do not think it is going to have any serious implications because it will in no way affect the price of the products and will in no way do what it is supposed to do, namely increase the amount of money which the farmers will receive for their products.
Of course it may have implications in a couple of the things which are proposed. One is a board and the other is an advisory committee. I am one who believes that the less the government interferes in the industrial life of a nation, the better that government is. Whenever I read about boards and advisory committees, I am just a little bit fearful. It reminds me of a statement that was made by a past president of the National Dairy Council of Canada who said that under various guises of assistance we are slowly being led more and more toward socialism and a socialistic state. The only implication which I see in this bill and upon which I look with a certain degree of fear is the appointment of boards and the appointment of advisory committees. Are we to assume that this advisory committee is going to tell the farmers what to


plant, how much to plant and so on? That could be one of the implications. It could mean further regimentation of the farmers and I believe we have too much of that in this country at the present time.
Another thing which he said-and in this I agree with him 100 per cent-was "I do not maintain it is a cure". I do not think it is even a panacea that you could give any credit for in any way whatever or by any stretch of the imagination. Then he mentioned something about the base price for any commodity and he said, "I want to stress that word 'any' ". I note that the minister is not in the house but I should like attention to be given to this question. When he speaks of a base price for any commodity I cannot help but wonder what action would be taken with regard to perishable products that are raised to such a great extent in our area. I am thinking of tomatoes which must be picked at a certain time or else. I am thinking of peaches, cherries, small fruits and the like of that and many vegetables. What is the action of a government board going to be with regard to removing a surplus of those products from the channels of trade and to supporting the price for them? I am just curious. I should like to know how it is going to be worked out.
Then in the case of overproduction-and that is a very ticklish question-what is to happen? There are a great many ideas about overproduction. We hear that there can never be such a thing as overproduction so long as people are going to bed hungry; and of course that is perfectly right. Technically it is sound. But nevertheless I maintain that there is overproduction when you have produced more than the home market can absorb and, on top of that, more than can be sold in the international markets of the world and then more than the people of Canada can afford to finance for the use of those unable to buy their own supplies. When we have reached that stage we have reached overproduction. It is quite possible that such a thing could happen.
These are some of the things that made me wonder what is going to be the result of this legislation that is supposed to cure the farmers' problem. We know that the farmers have a problem. We know that agriculture needs the attention of the government. However, it is not temporary policies that are needed. We have waited for so long for a cure that I think we shall be well advised to take a little bit more time at this period and see that the legislation which is approved by this house is really a cure for the troubles that are facing agriculture today. I maintain that the only way in which that can be done is as has been suggested by so many who have spoken and as

was so ably done by the hon. member lor Acadia this afternoon, and that is to see that this legislation is presented to the committee on agriculture of this house and that that committee is given ample time-not just the time between now and Christmas but all the time that is necessary-to see that proper and thorough consideration is given to any plan that will, we hope, assist agriculture and put it on a sound footing for years to come.
I think we are all in agreement with some few words that I am going to read from a book written by Lauren Soth. It is called "Farm Trouble". It is quite a simple title, is it not? There is certainly a great deal of trouble on the farm and among the farmers of the world today. Lauren Soth was born in Sibley in the United States 47 years ago and studied agricultural journalism at Iowa State College. He has been an associate professor at Iowa State College and editor of The Agricultural Situation in the United States Department of Agriculture and has held various positions in that department. I am telling hon. members that just to give them confidence, as I have, in some of the statements which he has made. In his last paragraph in the book he says this:
Americans-
I think we can substitute "Canadians" and agree 100 per cent with the wording as it is here.
-want farming to be a healthy industry and a satisfactory way of life. They want farmers to be paid by society in proportion to their contribution to society, as urban workers are. The same amount of skill and productivity ought to command the same income whether in farming or in steel making. But Americans do not want to adopt rigid government controls aimed at achieving this equality if these should mean sacrificing the initiative, the independence, and the freedom of the farm family.
With these words, Mr. Chairman, I think we are all in complete agreement. I do not believe that there is in Canada any other class of people or any other individuals who are so proud of their individual initiative and so jealous of their rights as individuals in this free enterprise economy. I am sure that it would be a sorry day whenever any government tried to regiment and to control the farmers of this country in order to give them what they think might be some assistance. The author of this book also has this to say about assistance at page 193:
If farmers are to receive income supplements, beyond what they receive in the market, then those supplements should be direct and unrelated to particular commodities.
After reading that statement, it is my opinion that this man must have made quite a study of Social Credit policy because that sentence is a clear-cut statement agreeing
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization with the whole Social Credit belief on national dividends. It is also a condemnation of direct subsidies and direct assistance in certain commodities that are put on the market for the nation. I am going to read that statement again:
If farmers are to receive income supplements, beyond what they receive in the market, then those supplements should be direct and unrelated to particular commodities.
This whole book is a very thorough review of what has taken place in the United States of America during the past 20 years and the various plans that have been adopted and tried out in order to improve the position of agriculture.

That is the plan to which the minister said this morning he had given such careful consideration-he had found some mistakes which he hoped to rectify. Well that is very good news, but according to this writer, who has made a very careful study of this whole situation, it has been just one series of mistakes after another.

I would like to say a few more words, however, on this question of the farming troubles at the present time. In the end, it is one way of seeing that those people whose incomes do not reach a certain level are provided with sufficient to guarantee them the necessities of life.
Now we go on to consider what is the duty of the government. I was quite interested in a little booklet the other day, put out by the Canadian chamber of commerce, and on page 4 therein we find this statement:
It believes-
Here it is speaking of the chamber-
-that the role of government in economic affairs should be to stimulate development, to ease the impacts of economic fluctuation and to prohibit anti-social excesses.
Now that is something with which we can thoroughly agree. Of course, we have at the

We believe the position in agriculture today is due to the policies of this and the preceding governments in not bringing about the proper development of agriculture in this country in comparison with other industries which are developing at the present time.
My memory goes back quite a few years ago to the very first election in Canada of which I was aware, and that was the great reciprocity election of 1911. At that time I was not old enough to vote but I had just finished high school and thought I knew it all. Despite the fact that I had been raised in a very strong Liberal household, on that occasion I disagreed with those policies and felt that the imposition of a tariff was the only way in which we could develop and foster industry in Canada.
That was, as I say, my belief at that time and I know that very serious debates were then taking place regarding trade with England, trade with the United States and so on. In fact, when you see what is going on today there is quite a parallel between that year of 1911 and 1957. Be that as it may, a tariff policy developed in this country over the years which gave support to industries in Canada, with the exception of agriculture. Furthermore, by giving support to these various other industries it also tended to increase the prices of many things which our farmers had to buy in order to carry on their production.
I am just putting this forward as a suggestion; we are all trying to find a solution, but I am just wondering if the mistake did not occur in those years when we gave protection to all other industry in Canada by means of a tariff, but failed to do so in the case of agriculture. I can see no difference between a factory which is turning out a commodity for the retail trade and for the use of the people of Canada and the farmer who is turning out, or manufacturing if you will, commodities also for the use of the people of Canada. We have on the one hand industry protected by tariffs and on the other hand we have the farmer without any such protection.
We are also in agreement with the idea that tariff restriction and trade barriers should be done away with just as quickly as possible, but I still think we have to be realistic about the situation so long as we are living in a nation and in a world where tariff barriers do exist and where they are likely to continue to exist for generations to come. I think this fact must be considered, and I therefore make the suggestion that,


if this problem ever gets before the agricultural committee, would it not be well that this government and this parliament should consider some method by which assistance could be given to agriculture by way of tariff protection.
There are many instances which I could cite right in my own area. For instance, when the influx of soft fruit from across the line gets too serious we then have seasonal tariffs imposed. We deal with the case of vegetables in the same way. I am wondering if it would not be a good idea to have that kind of planning extended to give greater protection to other commodities.
As I said, we have these problems in other parts of the country. There is the question of hay. In my own area, which is the northern part of Okanagan, I understand according to word recently received, that we have 2,000 tons of hay for which the growers cannot find a market. This situation prevails at a time when hay is still coming into our Fraser valley area-the coast area of British Columbia-from the United States. It is being trucked across on large trailers and delivered direct to the farmer. They even have elevators which will put the bales up in the farmer's hay loft, and that hay, after paying a duty of $1.06 per ton is delivered right to the farmer's barn-

Then there is no allowance made for bad weather which we sometimes experience in the Okanagan, and so farmers lose their crops. This is what farmers are up against. There is a tariff of $1.06 a ton. Why can that tariff not be raised so that the farmers in the Okanagan can supply hay, and compete with the United States grower in the Fraser valley? I am throwing this suggestion out for consideration when this bill comes before the committee on agriculture.
There has been a lot of discussion about taking land out of production. We maintain that it is not humane to curtail the production of food as long as there is hunger in the world. Nevertheless, I am going to read part of an article I got from a newspaper yesterday. It appears under a Washington dateline, and it reads:
The committee for economic development says more land and people in the United States need to be taken out of farming.
Present price-depressing surpluses and the low level of income of many farmers reflect the existence of too much productive capacity, the CED said yesterday in a report prepared by one of its committees.
And this report goes on to say:
The CED is a private research agency sponsored by 150 leading industrial leaders and educationists. Its declared purpose is to help boost United States productivity and standard of living. CED describes itself as a non-partisan non-profit organization.
There is some doubt with relation to the amount of land which should be under production, and it is the opinion of this committee that it should be curtailed. The problem arises: How are you going to do this and what means are you going to adopt? This is another subject which should be discussed and agreed on by the committee on agriculture before any legislation is presented for adoption.
So, Mr. Chairman, I make a strong plea that these matters should be considered in committee. We are now laying down plans which we hope will be permanent; we hope they will do the job which is necessary, and which it is intended they should do, that is to place the farmers of this country on a par with their neighbouring cousins in towns and cities, and on a par with the industrialists and manufacturers who are doing such a fine job in putting before us the necessities of life which we can produce in such abundance.

This evening I want to refer to fruits and vegetables. I come from the Niagara district where many fruits and vegetables are grown. In looking over the former legislation and former discussions in this house back over the years, I see that it has been the concern of many governments. I refer to the marketing troubles of the fruit and vegetable growers. I noticed in reading over old Hansards that the Hon. J. D. Chaplin, who was the member for Lincoln and the minister of trade and commerce in Mr. Meighen's administration, spoke at considerable length on fruit and vegetables. In the main, these producers were generally at a marked disadvantage against competition from similar fruits and vegetables from the United States where the season is always more advanced and consequently the fruits and vegetables from there reach the market sooner than ours.
Hon. Charles Dunning, in introducing his budget on May 1, 1930, said that seasonal tariffs alone were not applicable to Canada because of its extremes of distance, latitude and the climate. After a careful study at that time he decided to put on two duties, an ad valorem and specific duty. He hoped that this combination of duties would meet, first, the urgent need of the producers and help them to establish their prices at a time when they had an acute instability of price and, second, he hoped also that it would at the same time guarantee to the consumers that they would have these products at reasonable prices at all seasons of the year.
This combination of duties was intended to give our fruit and vegetable producers the greatest protection at the time of the harvest of their primary products. The time of application of the double duty was made to correspond with the Canadian harvest of the particular fruit or vegetable on which protection was meant to be given. As an example, if peaches ripened and were harvested over a nine weeks period the seasonal duty applied for nine weeks. This type of 96698-142*
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization protection was given to different fruits and vegetables for a certain definite period for each and the beginning of a period was generally announced in advance by the government after consultation with the growers themselves.
These flexible periods of extra seasonal tariffs do not always work out to the advantage of the growers. We had an example of this last spring. Our asparagus was ready for harvesting before it was expected and much United States asparagus was being imported right up to the time our asparagus was ready for the market. I was told that the former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, made the seasonal tariff period correspond with that asked for by the growers themselves. But we had a particularly warm spell and our asparagus was ready early. Often our growers cannot be expected to foretell the beginning and duration of any particular harvest because of our weather which varies from year to year. For this and other reasons which I can best illustrate with the harvesting of peaches, the duration of the time of application by the government of the various seasonal tariffs on the different fruits and vegetables is not sufficiently long.
As I said earlier, peaches have a seasonal tariff period of nine weeks. This is not long enough, for two reasons. The first one is modern refrigeration. Because of adequate cold storage, peaches can be imported into Canada before ours are ripe and can be kept in cold storage and compete with our early varieties. At the end of the season peaches can be stored in cold storage in the state of New York and those peaches are subsidized. Often when there is a large crop there peaches are brought into Canada right after the seasonal tariff is removed. I have seen this happen. In past years I have seen our canners in the Niagara district canning United States peaches that were admitted into Canada right after our seasonal tariff was removed and our own superior peaches were left to rot on the ground.
Again, in recent years our own peach growers have developed new varieties and the peach crop ripens over a longer period than nine weeks. Cold storage has had the effect of contracting the nine weeks seasonal protection to six or seven weeks, and quite apart from the longer ripening season of the different varieties of peaches this makes the nine week period decided upon years ago seem quite unrealistic today. This same condition applies to some of our other fruits and vegetables.
Another matter that has been brought to my attention in connection with peaches is

I know that the Prime Minister said in Wallaceburg that Canada must make an active effort to regain its best markets in the commonwealth and at the same time protect its domestic markets for Canadian producers. Mr. Chairman, a great number of people in my riding have been waiting for some time for this resolution to be introduced. I think the minister probably gave a fuller explanation of the resolution than is normally done and I am assuming that he has pretty well explained what will be in the bill. A few weeks ago a crack was made about there not being any C.C.F. farm representatives from Ontario. There are three C.C.F. members now from Ontario and I should like to inform those unenlightened members that each of the three members has a large farming area in his constituency.
I represent the riding of Timiskaming. May I say, for the benefit of those who are unaware of the situation, that this riding contains a unique geographical phenomena called the little clay belt. This little clay belt contains about one million acres of farm land. Fifty or sixty years ago this land was covered with timber. The governments of the day put on a drive, as they did in the west, and invited pioneers to come in and homestead. This event occurred about the same time as it did in the west. My father, a very young man at the time, went into northern Ontario by steamer, since there were no roads or railroads. In 1898 these pioneers cleared that land and today there are about 300,000 taxable acres of farm land in Timiskaming.
This clay land is probably as good land as you have anywhere in the country. It is fairly flat, being the bottom of an old lake in an earlier geological age. There are approximately 105,000 acres of this land under active field cultivation, and about 25 per cent of the total area of the clay belt is now cleared. This clay belt is almost entirely in the riding of Timiskaming and it supports some 100,000 people on approximately 1,600 farms according to the last census. There are 400 farm families living on that land. About 1,000 of the farms, like the farms

throughout Ontario and the rest of Canada, are lying idle. There are only 400 of these farms, as I said, that are supporting people who live by farming alone. There are others who are living on the farm and working elsewhere or deriving the majority of their income from other sources. I would suggest that this is an odd situation in a country which has the facility and the people. The people who went into my particular part of the country must have liked farming because they did go to the trouble of clearing the land in order to farm. They came there, worked and pioneered and now they are unable to derive sufficient income. I think it is about time the Canadian people took a look at the situation and wondered why these events have occurred.
We have a problem in Timiskaming that I think is the same as elsewhere. We have probably 25,000 head of cattle and a large beef section which sells between 4,000 and
5,000	head a year. This area supplies a large amount of fluid milk. We have a dairy industry, and the surprising thing about this dairy industry, to those who have never heard of Timiskaming, is that it produces half the amount of the butter that Canada exported last year. I do not say that all the butter that came from my area was exported, but we produced half of the total butter exported. We produced a large amount of cheese. We could easily have supplied all the butter and all the cheese that Canada exported. This is a surprising fact when one considers that it would come from one riding, and from a riding which many people did not know was a farming area. We have four butter factories, one each at Belle Vallee, Englehart, New Liskeard and Earlton. These four factories produce half of the amount exported according to the figures presented by the Ontario government in their statistical report.
We might wonder why people are leaving their farms. Farm organizations are continually making representations to the governments. The governments must be aware there is a farm problem. About 65 per cent of the members of this house are in this house because farmers elected them. It may be true, in fact it is true, that the farm population of Canada is small in numbers. It is true also that this farm population has the means of deciding through their elected representatives, upon the legislation affecting them to be passed by this house. I suggest that this government had better take a very close look at the situation because I do not think the proposed measure offers any solution.

It may only mean, Mr. Chairman, that one is a little smarter than the other. Frankly, I believe that a good look should be taken at this question of parity prices. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has just presented a document-I do not know whether or not you would call it a brief-addressed to the members of the House of Commons.
I presume it was also presented to the government. They ask for a level of farm supports and they go on to say that "they should not be set at less than 70 per cent of parity, as we calculate it by the formula which we have adopted". They do not include the formula that they adopted. If they did so, it would not make a hoot of difference because why should we take 70 per cent of parity when it means that you are going to have to find 30 per cent some place else in order to finance your operation? Any farmer who goes out and produces anything at any amount less than parity is going to have to subsidize it. How is he going to subsidize it? Is he going to get relief from his municipality? Is he going to have child labour? Is he going to make his kids work for nothing or is he going to work himself for nothing?
I suggest that one of the things the farmer has been doing for a great number of years has been living on his depreciation. He may not have known that he should have put it away but he has certainly been living on it. We can go right back to the hungry thirties and probably up to the time price control came on in 1940, when the farmer had lived on his depreciation. His machinery was falling apart, his buildings were falling down and his house had not had a coat of paint for many years. Times got a little better with price control and times got a little better just after the war, in fact, and continued up until 1951, and the farmer bought more machinery. He did put away a little bit of his depreciation.
But that certainly is not happening now. He has not been putting very much away since 1951 or else the farmer is giving me a poor story. As I understand it, most of them are not putting anything away, have taken out all that they have saved in what they considered to be the good years and it is time that we did something for those farmers. If this government wishes to stay in office, I think it had better do so now because 65 per cent of the members that are here are going to have to answer to those farmers.
There are some things that have been put under parity. I am sure that some of the

members will say it has not been applied. It has been applied in Ontario by the one organization that I know of that has ever been very active on its own, in making its own presentation and making its own way in Ontario,-I refer to the Ontario whole milk producers league-particularly in the fluid milk field. They have a parity formula. I do not necessarily agree with this formula because I do not know whether or not they set their price originally high enough. But they make use of a number of indexes.
I suggest that the minister listen to this and maybe take a pattern off it. They have a wholesale index and that is 20 per cent. They have a weekly wages index and that is 20 per cent. They have a commodities and services used by farmers index and that is 30 per cent; price of butterfat index, 10 per cent; price of condensed products index, 10 per cent; price of cheese index, 10 per cent. These amount to a total of 100 per cent. It is 100 per cent of a number of indexes of the commodities that go to make up the production costs of the fluid milk product. They take this price. They put their base price over 100 times the amount and they come up with a figure. They say that they will use a three months' period for setting their price and if the formula increases, it will increase by 19 cents a hundred, calculated on a three months' period. I am not suggesting that this particular price is the right one. The original base was 1949 to 1952 and the price in Toronto was $4.13; in 1953 it was $4.63; in 1954 I believe it was $4.53; in 1956 it was $4.77. It can therefore be seen that it has some relationship. Whether or not it is the right relationship, it has some relationship to the cost of that product. They have a signed contract yearly, signed by the Ontario whole milk producers' league and by A. P. Clark, the secretary for the government. I suggest that there is no question about it but that this would solve the problem for agriculture.
One of the arguments continually used against using a formula price or a full parity price is the fact that we may have surpluses. Mr. Chairman, we may not have surpluses now but we certainly have a problem. Under the former government we were buying from other countries more than we were selling. I understand that we now have a $1 billion dollar deficit this year already. I suggest that we cannot overproduce all the products that are derived from agriculture. I say that because I have heard on numerous occasions outstanding speakers like C. H. Millard, who is with the I.C.F.T.U., say so. I have heard him on numerous occasions after returning from Asia, Africa and the countries of Europe tell of the need for food commodities in those

countries. He told us of the children who never in their lifetime have ever had a full meal. I always thought we got these stomachs because we ate too much. It may be in some cases because we did not eat enough. Children are being born, are living a lifetime and are dying-very young-never having had a full meal in their lifetime. I suggest that we can do as much for peace by filling their hungry stomachs and bringing them to our way of thinking as we can by stockpiling arms in Canada or building radar units or doing the other silly things that we do for defence.
We have also heard that if we are going to have a decent price for agriculture we are going to end up in the same position as the United States. May I say that I think some of our farmers would be very happy tonight if they thought we were going to end up with as much money from farm products as they have in the United States.

We cannot sit in our seats in the house here and say, "They may come to us to buy our wheat". We had an opportunity to sell wheat to Australia. The minister was given this information very early in the session and he tried to make a joke of our selling wheat to Australia. We should have had an attache down there trying to sell that wheat, taking whatever currency we could get, so that we can eliminate this deficit we have in trade and accumulate a little bit of a surplus. We are not finding our farmers very happy about the situation they have, where the surplus is being carried on their farms. I think it is time that the surplus was carried on the books of the government and used for international trade.
We have heard many times-I hear it from the benches across the aisle-that the people will not stand for this, that prices are going to go up. My hon. friend on the other side of
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the house tonight quoted from a book, "Memorandum to the Government of Canada" from the Canadian Labour Congress, an organization of which I am proud to be a member, and they had something to do with this in the past. He read a statement. I think that statement should be read again. It is as follows:
We are alarmed by the drastic fall in farm income. This is bad for the farm people, most of whom are far from rich, and who still make up one-sixth of the Canadian population. It is bad for the economy generally, which is still heavily dependent on exports, of which farm products make up about one-quarter.
And I would add that they should be making up about three-quarters.
It is also bad for Canadian workers, for whose products a prosperous agriculture would provide a substantial market.
Then it goes on to say this:
Canadian labour will fully support anything the government can do to restore the purchasing power of Canadian farmers.
Well, now we know exactly what the workers think about increasing the prosperity of the farms, and let me tell you they are not doing it because they are completely unselfish, they are doing it because they know that the farmer is now getting less than 43 per cent of the consumer dollar. They know, furthermore, that sales of automobiles are dropping; that sales of farm machinery are dropping; they know that these problems exist and they are willing to help their friends in the rural areas who are in the agricultural field.
I say that the government, knowing that these people must have at least 2J dependents like everybody else and that they represent a very large part of the economy of Canada, and in view of the fact that they have been given the green light, now have no reason for sitting still and saying that the people might not go for it. We have very many other problems in agriculture, apart from the fact that we have to supply these people who are producing the agricultural products with a decent income. I think that can be done by parity prices. I think we should get straight with regard to this business of parity prices and I do not think we should continually change the name. When I find the meaning of parity prices I am not too happy about the term being changed to deficiency payments and so on-1 am quite sure that this viewpoint is shared by farm organizations and others-because then it means that they have to sit down and find out the meaning of deficiency payments.
However, as I say, there are other problems. For instance we have in my area a number of beef cattle and we ship these cattle to Toronto. I think this government

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization should put in a grading station and an abattoir so that we will be able to supply good beet for the markets in that particular area, which is already consuming much more than we can produce. Yet while our local product is going on the Toronto market it is not going to local markets. Of course, other markets constitute another problem in which I think this government should also get involved. We hear such statements as: "Oh, packinghouses, they are wonderful things; they only make .4 per cent profit", or something of that nature. They make very little profit.
Now when we take one of the largest packinghouses, which incidentally sends me its financial statement, it looks just about as nice as the financial statements of the mining organizations in which I used to work. That was in the gold mining industry and the financial statement to which I have referred reminds me of that. They show shares valued at $1,438,284 and the dividend this year on that .4 per cent which they were supposed to be making was $1,050,000. Now, what we do not know is that the Canadian people have financed this organization to a great extent, because they already have the accumulated capital invested in the way of land, buildings, and so on, assets to the value of $62 million and something. They have another $62 million which they call current assets. Then they point out how you can only make a very little bit of profit in that business.
Now I am sure that we as workers and we as farmers know that this problem has been raised continually. It has been raised by local newspapers on the rural scene which we are sometimes foolish to read and which say the farmer is the enemy of labour and labour is the enemy of the farmer. Well labour, as I said, has said what they think about the farmer. They are willing to cooperate and in some ways they have done so. For instance, in connection with the setting up of the joint economic commission. They have co-operated and are getting along very well.
It is true that when I was a miner and I sent my wife down to the local store with $5, she could buy a very small roast. She would think that the father-in-law had a big farm with a big cow and so there must be a hundred of those $5 roasts in that big cow. So she was of the opinion that the farmer was doing darn good. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have had a very wide and general range of debate on agriculture today. I doubt whether a good deal of it was in order in a discussion of this resolution. However, I did not raise a point of order except when hon. members got onto fisheries or something along that line. However, we have heard speeches here today in connection with the question of tariffs, in connection with the financial setup of a certain company and in connection with all kinds of individual agricultural problems in particular areas or constituencies. A great deal of the content of the speeches has been concerned with the difficulties which exist in agriculture and with which farmers find themselves faced. Now I do not think there is any need for us to continue hearing speaker after speaker reiterating the difficult situation in agriculture today. I think most of us realize and have realized the situation for a considerable time, and one thing I can assure all hon. members of this house is that nobody realizes the situation as well as I do.

In the five or six months since I have been Minister of Agriculture I have had delegations from, I think, practically every producer group of any size and most of the smaller ones in this country. They have all come to me and told me their troubles, and as a result of that and of I do not know how many hundreds or thousands of letters from individuals and every conceivable organization, I think I do realize the situation in agriculture today and the difficulties involved, as to the industry on the whole right across Canada and as far as particular segments are concerned, as well as anybody else in this house.
Now the legislation which is presently before us is designed to try to improve that situation to some extent. When I spoke first this morning in introducing this resolution I tried to make it plain-and I should like to state again what I said then-that I did not look upon this as a cure-all for the many difficulties from which agriculture is suffering. I said at that time:
I do not maintain that it is a cure-all for all the difficulties under which agriculture has laboured for the past several years. No one piece of legislation can be expected, at one stroke, to transform a complex industry, such as agriculture, from a depressed state to one of full and abounding health.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
I realize the situation in this regard as well as anybody else does, but unfortunately most of the speeches we have heard here today have been along the line that by passing some piece of legislation we are going to wave a magic wand over the agricultural industry, and that as a result of waving this wand all the difficulties which confront it are going to disappear. That essentially has been the complaint of hon. members in the C.C.F. group and of some other hon. members who have spoken today. This legislation is not a cure-all. Nobody ever said it would be a cure-all, and nobody with any sense of realism as far as agriculture is concerned in this country can ever expect that any one piece of legislation would be a cure-all.
Mr. Chairman, in order to put agriculture on a sound basis and in order to give our farmers a reasonable standard of living we have to move forward on a considerable number of fronts. We are not confining action to this front alone.

We in this government are making every effort possible to move forward on a considerable number of fronts. I would just like to indicate some of the things we are engaged in doing which are necessary to restore agriculture to a sound position. First of all, we have to dispose of the big surplus of wheat which is hanging like a blanket over the price of agricultural products of all kinds in this country. That is one of the things, particularly, which has to be done before the agricultural industry in this country can be put on a sound basis, whether it is wheat raising or some type of agriculture in the maritimes. We are making every effort possible to dispose of this surplus of grain and, as indicated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, and as I can assure hon. members now, we are making some progress in that regard and we hope to reduce this surplus to at least a reasonable extent during the coming six months.
The second way in which we are trying to attack this problem is through the royal commission on price spreads which was announced here yesterday.

These aTe only some of the ways in which progress has to be made before agriculture can be put on a reasonable basis. We realize that there are many other things to be done in addition to this before we can get this industry into the situation we would like to see it in, and in which, I know, every hon. member in this house would like to see it.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, of all the criticism which has been put forward here today, hardly any of it was constructive. All we have heard from speaker after speaker was the terrible situation the farmer is in. We know the situation has been bad, but scarcely one speaker has made any suggestion as to how it could be improved.

I have not time to go over all the points which were made by the various speakers on the other side of the house, but I will attempt to deal with a few of them. First, the right hon. member for Melville: most of what he said was a defence of what the Liberal administration, of which he was a member, had done in the past. I do not blame him a bit for that; I think it is quite natural. But there is one statement he made to which I must take exception, and that is there is not much difference between this legislation and the legislation which he sponsored-the resolution of 1944, as he called it, setting up the prices support board. There are very many material differences between that legislation and this legislation which is projected, and I should like to outline briefly what some of them are.
First, this legislation provides for a definite formula to be used in the fixing of guaranteed and floor prices. Secondly, it provides under the legislation for an advisory committee which must be set up representing farmer organizations for the purpose of giving advice to the minister and the government in regard to what commodities should be under price support and the level of support which should be provided for them.

The third difference is that this legislation provides for guaranteed prices on any agricultural products, which are set for a year in advance. In other words this meets the demand for forward pricing. Some people have said the measure contains nothing about forward pricing. This legislation provides for a price to be set, and it is to be in effect for a year from that time. Also, this legislation provides for floor prices guaranteed by the legislation itself.

subtopic: C.N.R. LAY-OFFS, WINNIPEG
C.N.R. LAY-OFFS, WINNIPEG
speechtext:
North):
1.	Is a progressive lay-off taking place in the Canadian National Railways shops in Winnipeg?
2.	If so, how many men have been laid off by months since May 1, 1957?
3.	Was there an undertaking by the government that a works program would be instituted by the Canadian National Railways to protect those threatened by unemployment?
4.	If so, what is the present situation regarding this program?
Answer by: Mr. MacDonald, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
1.	In a statement made in the house on behalf of the Canadian National Railways on November 4, 1957, at page 704 of Hansard in reply to questions by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and other hon. members, the management dealt fully with the matter of adjustments in the number of employees on the system as a whole, and this statement is explanatory of the situation at Winnipeg.
2.	The average level of employment in the Winnipeg area from May to September was
as follows:
May	 3,054
June	 3,050
July	 3,048
August	 2,964
September	 2,926
3.	The government undertook to finance the cost of a special program of car repairs and other shop work as outlined in a press announcement issued from Ottawa by the Minister of Transport under date of July 12, 1957. The announcement also indicated that the Canadian National management would open conversations with union leaders to explore the adjustments in the existing seniority rules of the working groups affected which would be required to make the special program effective.
Questions
4.	Under date of August 26, 1957, the following press release was issued in Montreal: "The special work program aimed at minimizing the effect of lay-offs in C.N.R. shops, and announced by the Minister of Transport on July 12, has not been put into effect, the railway said today. A company statement explained: Following discussions with representatives of the unions it was found that transfers of workers between shop groups could not be provided for under the seniority rules that are part of the wage agreements".
